\viewkind4\uc1\pard\kerning2\f0\fs24 Mayor Trantalis explained the intent of this Agenda item is for the Commission is to select a proposal from the three (3) applicants.\par
\par
City Manager Williams explained that additional information from staff was provided to the Commission based on their feedback at the December 16, 2025, Commission Conference Meeting and expounded on related information and details.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis noted that the Commission requested a true side-by-side cost comparison with no changes to scope or design. Tonight\rquote s presentations are for clarification only, not revised proposals, to ensure the Commission\rquote s decision is based on comparable, consistent cost information. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Ben Rogers, Assistant City Manager, noted that staff standardized the proposals by requiring clear, all-inclusive cost assumptions to ensure comparable pricing. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Glassman's observation that the two (2) proposers\rquote numbers remained essentially unchanged and Park Place Garages, LLC\rquote s (PPG) proposal, decreased by roughly $11,000,000 and inquired about how that was possible given disclaimer language, Mr. Rogers remarked on staff efforts with the proposers. Commissioner Glassman said he would address this issue during proposer presentations.\i\par
\par
\i0 Mayor Trantalis recognized Gerry Guenther, G3 Development (G3) Managing Principal.\i \i0 Mr. Guenther, along with G3 members Scott Zdroik and Jacob Lucky narrated a presentation entitled \i HOLIDAY PARK PARKING GARAGE by G3 Development.\par
\par
\b A copy of the presentation is attached to this Agenda item.\b0 \par
\par
\i0 In response to Mayor Trantalis' questions, Mr. Guenther explained how the G3 proposal achieved the same parking count in fewer stories, which maximizes footprint efficiency, while meeting fire apparatus needs and commented on related information.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Glassman's question, Mr. Guenther described their experience delivering Fire-EMS stations that include building Fire-EMS facilities for Central Florida municipalities.\par
\par
Commissioner Glassman referenced the Commission consensus from a prior meeting favoring a fully built-out fire station, rather than delivering only a shell and completing the build-out later, and said that a start-to-finish, turnkey approach makes sense. \par
\par
In response to Commissioner Glassman's question regarding how a turnkey approach impacts price, Mr. Guenther said that their proposal assumes a turnkey, fully built-out fire station.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Sorensen's questions, Mr. Lucky confirmed his individual meetings with Mayor Trantalis and Commissioner Glassman. The G3 team has not yet met with neighborhood groups. Should the G3 Team be selected, neighborhood outreach would be an early priority.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Sorensen's question regarding whether the project can accommodate stormwater needs, Mr. Lucky explained that final stormwater design will be determined through detailed engineering calculations, confirmed they have significant experience integrating stormwater infrastructure into structured parking projects, and cited examples. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Glassman's questions regarding integrating the fire station within the parking garage structure, Fire-Rescue Department Chief Stephen Gollan emphasized that his primary concern is maintaining the operational integrity of the station and remarked on potential issues related to road noise and vehicle proximity and vibration from traffic above the sleeping quarters, Chief Gollan confirmed that G3 provided confidence with planned mitigation measures. Chief Gollan confirmed that secure parking requirements for firefighters under their collective bargaining agreement have been addressed in the G3 proposal. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Beasley-Pittman's question, Mr. Lucky confirmed that costs to address the parking garage's stormwater needs are included in their proposal.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Sorensen's question regarding life-cycle costs for the parking garage, Mr. Lucky explained their team draws on experience and feedback from past projects to improve and reduce long-term life cycle issues, including how materials and design choices affect long-term maintenance.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis expressed concern that G3's design was not adequately integrated into the park environment and discussed his viewpoint. Mr. Lucky noted flexibility regarding incorporating a mix of materials to soften the structure\rquote s appearance and discussed related information. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis commented that the other proposers devoted greater effort and resources to incorporating architectural and design elements that better integrate the parking garage into park surroundings. He noted that their lower cost proposal appeared to be for a more basic garage that did not include the same level of exterior design features of other proposals.\par
\par
Mr. Lucky acknowledged that their proposal emphasized a heavier investment in landscaping versus exterior architectural fa\'e7ade treatments and noted the ability to reallocate costs toward an enhanced exterior fa\'e7ade design. Further comment and discussion ensued regarding G3\rquote s design rendering and cost differences among the three (3) proposals.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Cody Kiess, CORE Construction President, on behalf of Holiday Park Parking Partners, LLC (HPPP). Mr. Kiess, along with HPPP Team Member Greg Kimmelman narrated a presentation entitled \i City of Fort Lauderdale Holiday Park Garage.\par
\par
\b A copy of the presentation is attached to this Agenda item.\b0\par
\i0\par
In response to Mayor Trantalis' questions, Mr. Kiess confirmed the cost amounts included in their presentation. Mr. Kiess explained that the vertiport, valued at approximately $16,000,000, would be privately funded, and would increase the overall project value. Mr. Kiess clarified related details and information. Mayor Trantalis confirmed his understanding.\par
\par
Commissioner Glassman noted that the HPPP team interacted with the presidents of Flagler Village and Victoria Park neighborhood associations, and its proposal included infrastructure to mitigate Victoria Park stormwater issues and enhance pedestrian connectivity from Flagler Village to Holiday Park.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Glassman's question regarding HPPP's higher proposal cost and not including the vertiport component, Mr. Kiess said that HPPP's proposal cost for the fire station and surface parking lot were generally consistent. The higher parking garage cost component primarily relates to intentional architectural, aesthetic, and urban-design choices, including smaller footprint, enhanced fa\'e7ade, and park-sensitive integration, not higher baseline construction costs.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Glassman's questions, Mr. Kiess reiterated that the vertiport would be privately funded at no cost to the City and its inclusion would be at the City\rquote s discretion. Mr. Kiess said that the vertiport space is designed to be adaptable, allowing future conversion to parking at no cost to the City.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Glassman's questions regarding an estimated $200,000 per year in lease revenue for the vertiport. Mr. Kiess explained that this figure was a preliminary estimate discussed between the financing partner and VertiPorts by Atlantic (VBA). The lease would be subject to negotiations during the comprehensive agreement phase and explained related information.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Glassman's question regarding how HPPP's proposal compares to G3 and PPG\rquote s proposals, excluding the vertiport component, Mr. Kiess said that their proposal reflects additional planning and site details, including a dedicated rideshare pickup area, enhanced landscaping with mature trees, and a strong emphasis on protecting existing native trees. \par
\par
In response to Commissioner Glassman's questions, Mr. Kiess reiterated that the $16,000,000 vertiport deck value reflects a defined construction cost not funded by the City and confirmed that the vertiport lease revenues would be negotiated. Financial and operational risk related to the vertiport is placed on the private tenant.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Glassman's question regarding why the Commission would not select the lowest cost proposal, Mr. Kiess explained that though a lower-cost pared down garage proposal is available, HPPP's proposal delivers superior long-term value through design quality, connectivity, user amenities, and a more holistic park-centered P3 approach.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Sorensen's question regarding who would be responsible for operating and maintaining the vertiport, Mr. Kiess said that all operations and maintenance of the vertiport would be the responsibility of VBA, the tenant. The City would be the lessor with no operational or maintenance costs for the vertiport area of the Garage.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Sorensen's question regarding VBA's experience with similar facilities, Mr. Kiess said that vertiports are an emerging industry. The proposed vertiport facility would be the first of its kind in the United States, although similar vertiports are being operated in the Middle East.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Sorensen's question, Mr. Kiess reconfirmed that vertiport space is designed to be adaptable, allowing future conversion to parking spaces, at no cost to the City.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Sorensen's question regarding the Garage\rquote s maintenance and life-cycle costs, Mr. Kiess explained the City's option to participate in an operations and maintenance (O&M) component supported by a national parking infrastructure operator. Should the City elect to opt out of that component, the City will assume responsibility for O&M of the Garage areas used for vehicle parking. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Beasley-Pittman's questions regarding the proposed vertiport, Roly Tapanes, VBA Southeast Regional Vice President, explained the proposed vertiport is part of a broader South Florida location model and cited examples. The Fort Lauderdale vertiport location would be directly connected to those regional sites, including Fort Lauderdale Executive Airport (FXE), and explained related information.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Sorensen's question regarding costs should the City elect to opt into the O&M component, Mr. Kiess said those costs would be outside the previously referenced $41,000,000 and he could provide that information.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Beasley-Pittman's question regarding the State of Florida and the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Mr. Tapanes explained information associated with required FAA approvals and remarked on the State's proactive involvement. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Beasley-Pittman's questions regarding the Fire-EMS Station location in the HPPP proposal, Mr. Kiess explained that their proposal includes a drive-through fire station immediately adjacent to the Garage, within the same overall project footprint, and discussed related information.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Herbst remarked on his viewpoint that HPPP's proposal is the only true public-private partnership (P3) due to its revenue-sharing structure. He cautioned that the long-term revenue should be evaluated on a net present value basis, which significantly reduces its effective financial impact, and remarked on his viewpoint.\par
\par
In response to Vice Mayor Herbst's question, Mr. Kiess confirmed that City and proposer financial obligations are separate. The City would fund its portion of the Garage, while the proposer would independently finance its share of the vertiport. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
In response to Vice Mayor Herbst's question, Mr. Kiess acknowledged and discussed information related to early termination of the vertiport component, which would require negotiated compensation. Further comment and discussion ensued regarding the related agreement and a reasonable period to recover its vertiport investment. \par
\par
Vice Mayor Herbst expounded on his viewpoint regarding the FAA approval timeframe of vertiports, viability of the vertiport business model, and related opportunities. Mr. Kiess addressed concerns about the pace of adoption of new aviation technology, its implications for the overall project, and said that the project\rquote s financial and operational assumptions address those concerns. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
In response to Vice Mayor Herbst's questions regarding the scenario should the vertiport operation fail, Mr. Kiess said that the City would regain the top deck as conventional parking at no conversion cost. The vertiport operator, VBA, would commit to restoring the area to conventional parking, estimated at approximately two hundred (200) parking spaces. Mr. Kiess noted that specific financial guarantees for that obligation would need to be negotiated to ensure adequate protection for the City. Mr. Kiess noted one (1) option under consideration would pre-fund the conversion cost into initial financing. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
In response to Vice Mayor Herbst's question regarding the noise impact of air taxis utilizing the vertiport on the Police horses residing at Holiday Park, Mr. Kiess discussed related decibel levels and noise mitigation options. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
In response to Vice Mayor Herbst's questions regarding the number of flights in VBA\rquote s business plan and hours of operation, Mr. Kiess said that the business plan assumes very low initial flight activity with gradual growth over several years and daytime-only operations.\par
\par
In response to Vice Mayor Herbst's question regarding the flight paths and public safety, Mr. Kiess said that flight paths would be determined by the FAA and that preliminary assumed flight paths over Sunrise Boulevard and transitioning over the ocean. \par
\par
Vice Mayor Herbst remarked on HPPP\rquote s involvement with the new City Hall project. In response to Vice Mayor Herbst's question regarding adequate staffing and management capacity for the Garage project, Mr. Kiess confirmed sufficient staffing, cited examples, and emphasized that efforts will not be compromised by concurrent projects. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recessed the meeting at 8:27 p.m.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis reconvened the meeting at 8:40 p.m.\par
\par
City Manager Williams remarked on a potential overlap with the Garage project and the LauderTrail project. Mr. Rogers provided an update on the portion of the LauderTrail project that advances its segment along Federal Highway to War Memorial Auditorium and extending to NE 9th Avenue is fully designed, funded, and ready for construction. \par
\par
In response to Commissioner Glassman's question about the segment of LauderTrail along the west side of Federal Highway near the former Searstown site, Mr. Rogers explained that segment is partially planned, with specifications developed, but implementation is tied to the Searstown redevelopment.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized John Scherer, Park Place Garages, LLC (PPG). In response to Mayor Trantalis' question regarding the $11,000,000 decrease in their proposal, Mr. Scherer clarified that the price did not drop but was the result of removing non-comparable scope items from its proposal. Mr. Scherer along with PPG Team members Rob Gillette, and Merrill Romanik narrated a presentation entitled \i Holiday Park Parking Garage & Fire Station.\i0 \par
\par
\b\i A copy of the presentation is attached to this Agenda item.\b0\i0\par
\par
In response to Mayor Trantalis' question, Mr. Scherer clarified the location and function of the landscaped area shown in their rendering is on the south side of the Garage. Mayor Trantalis noted that this proposal does not include removing existing trees.\par
\par
In response to Mayor Trantalis' question, Ms. Romanik confirmed that a covered pathway could be incorporated between the Garage and The Parker and explained related details. Further comment and discussion ensued regarding pedestrian travel at the site.\par
\par
Mr. Scherer introduced Mark Santos, Walker Consultants. Mr. Santos presented on Walker Consultants\rquote expertise in parking facility asset management and assisting owners plan realistic annual budgets to ensure long-term O&M.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Glassman's question regarding one (1) ingress and egress point in its rendering, Mr. Scherer explained that their design includes multiple access points, cited examples, and noted a dedicated valet circulation loop, which supports efficient traffic flow. Ms. Romanik noted the garage's two (2) points of ingress and egress and two (2) one-way travel paths accommodating valet service.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis noted that PPG\rquote s design still shows partially covered parking on the top level without a solar component that was included in PPG's initial presentation. In response to Mayor Trantalis' question regarding the cost of retaining that solar component, Mr. Scherer stated that the estimated cost to keep the solar component would be approximately $2,700,000.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Sorensen's question regarding PPG's advantages associated with PPG\rquote s ongoing work on the YMCA/Broward Health project and The Parker project if it were selected to build the Garage, Mr. Scherer explained that because the PPG team is delivering those projects, they bring proven, site-specific expertise in drainage, flood mitigation, and community coordination.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Glassman's question regarding clarification on revenue generation assumptions, how parking revenue would be generated and whether existing agreements limit the City\rquote s ability to charge for parking at The Parker and War Memorial events, Mr. Rogers explained that parking revenue for the Garage is uncertain, as existing agreements require parking availability but do not clearly allow fees. Mr. Rogers said any event-related revenue would be limited and insufficient to cover debt service, making the Parking Fund the primary funding source. Mr. Rogers said that a comprehensive parking study and policy direction on charging mechanisms are needed. Mr. Rogers confirmed staff is confident the City can operate and maintain the garage. \par
\par
Commissioner Glassman expressed concern about charging park users for parking, noting the difficulty of distinguishing park users from event patrons. Mr. Rogers outlined a range of possible tools to balance access and revenue generation, cited examples, and reiterated that parking revenue assumptions remain uncertain. \par
\par
In response to Commissioner Glassman's question regarding the viability of vertiports, Rufus James, Fort Lauderdale Executive Airport (FXE) Director, said that based on Fort Lauderdale\rquote s successful experience with helicopter operations and the growing momentum behind Electric Vertical Take-Off and Landing (eVTOL) technology, a vertiport is viewed as viable, forward-looking, beneficial, and cited examples of its ability to enhance regional connectivity. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Glassman's question about whether FXE has contemplated a vertiport, Mr. James explained that FXE has been constrained by a lack of suitable vacant land. Atlantic Aviation, an existing fixed-base operator (FBO) tenant at FXE is investing in related opportunities, which could accommodate a vertiport. Mr. James clarified that the primary role of FXE in an eVTOL network would be for aircraft support functions. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Glassman's question, Mr. James noted that industry discussions indicate strong national momentum for eVTOL technology, especially in congested metro areas. Mr. James noted that the City is well positioned to be an early, credible participant. In response to Commissioner Glassman's question regarding overall viability, Mr. James reaffirmed that he believes the proposed vertiport is a viable opportunity and cited related benefits.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Glassman's question regarding whether eVTOL aircraft use would be affordable, Mr. James explained that the long-term goal is for pricing to be comparable to premium Uber type services and remarked that over time, there would be broader acceptance and use with a defined market. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Herbst remarked on comparable helicopter transport services and examples of an elite class of users. Mr. James explained that eVTOL aircraft are expected to serve small groups seeking a shared, experience-driven form of travel that would be more accessible than traditional helicopter operations. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Herbst discussed his viewpoint regarding viability of the vertiport market, acknowledged support for the concept by federal and state governments but questioned whether the vertiport component would ultimately succeed. Further comment and discussion ensued regarding the Commission moving forward and ranking the three (3) garage proposals. \par
\par
Vice Mayor Herbst noted that the vertiport is a defining aspect of HPPP's proposal that fundamentally changes the nature and value of the HPPP proposal.\par
\par
Commissioner Glassman discussed the significance of the Garage site and the importance of overall quality. Commissioner Glassman commented on the attributes and configurations of each proposal, expounded on his support for the HPPP proposal and its ability to generate revenue, expounding on his viewpoint.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis discussed weighing and prioritizing the proposals factors, including cost, design quality, and potential revenue generation to best align with the priorities for Holiday Park. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Commissioner Glassman reiterated his support of the HPPP proposal, citing its outstanding design and their team's early community engagement that resulted in support from adjacent civic associations, and expounded on related information.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis noted that the vertiport revenue source is several years away. Further comment and discussion ensued. \par
\par
In response to Commissioner Glassman's question, Mr. Kiess remarked that City revenue from the vertiport could begin shortly after construction is complete through lease payments for the vertiport deck, even if full vertiport operations ramp up slowly. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
In response to Mayor Trantalis' remarks regarding the HPPP proposal, Commissioner Glassman explained his viewpoint that the higher cost of the HPPP proposal is justified because vertiport lease revenue can offset the price difference over time, reduce pressure to charge park users for parking, and adds long-term value. Commissioner Glassman reiterated neighborhood feedback and support and expounded on his perspective. Further comment and discussion ensued. \par
\par
City Attorney McCartney confirmed the need for the Commission to rank the three (3) proposals. Commissioner Glassman remarked on the ability for staff to negotiate cost-related items with the highest ranked proposer. \par
\par
Commissioner Glassman confirmed his ranking: HPPP ranked one (1); PPG ranked two (2); and G3 ranked three (3). \par
\par
Commissioner Beasley-Pittman confirmed her ranking: HPPP ranked one (1); G3 ranked two (2); and PPG ranked three (3).\par
\par
Vice Mayor Herbst confirmed his ranking: PPG ranked one (1); HPPP ranked two (2); and G3 ranked three (3). Vice Mayor Herbst explained his ranking, noting design aspects of the PPG proposal and discussed related information. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Commissioner Sorensen recommended that the process for the selected Garage proposal mirror the City Hall Process and include scope and cost negotiations to fit a defined budget without sacrificing core design or program objectives. \par
\par
In response to Commissioner Sorensen's question about affordability, City Manager Williams said that all the proposals are affordable, the G3 and PPG garage proposals are more closely aligned with the City\rquote s fiscal comfort level, particularly with respect to debt capacity and overall approach to financing the project. \par
\par
Mayor Trantalis remarked on the need to consider revenue generation from the HPPP proposal. City Manager Williams clarified the vertiport was not included in staff's like-to-like proposal comparison, explained staff's evaluation factors, and cited examples.\par
\par
In response to Mayor Trantalis' question regarding the previous January 2025 Design Criteria Package for the Garage, estimated at $37,000,000, included the parking garage, surface parking lot, and a Fire-EMS Station, Mr. Rogers said that the current garage estimates are in line with that prior cost estimate. However, the current design removed previous office space and added a Fire-EMS Station. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Commissioner Sorensen explained that he prefers vertiport lease payments to begin at certificate of occupancy. Mr. Kiess confirmed and noted it would need to be negotiated with the tenant, VBA. Commissioner Sorensen acknowledged that revenue remains viable. Commissioner Sorensen remarked on staff negotiations related to cost and design regardless of which proposal is selected. \par
\par
In response to Commissioner Sorensen's question, City Attorney McCartney confirmed during comprehensive agreement negotiations, either party could decline to move forward, and the next ranked proposal would begin negotiations with staff. \par
\par
In response to Commissioner Sorensen's question, City Manager Williams confirmed part of negotiating a comprehensive agreement would include determination of a fiscally acceptable budget that would include any potential revenue generated by the facility. \par
\par
Commissioner Sorensen emphasized that given the early and unproven nature of the vertiport concept, neighborhood support and community impact are a critical deciding factor. Further comment and discussion ensued. Commissioner Glassman reiterated support of adjacent neighborhoods.\par
\par
Commissioner Sorensen confirmed his ranking: HPPP ranked one (1); PPG ranked two (2); and G3 ranked three (3).\par
\par
\par
Vice Mayor Herbst made a motion to extend this meeting until 11:00 p.m. and was seconded by Commissioner Sorensen.\par
\b\par

\par

\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis confirmed his ranking: HPPP ranked one (1); PPG ranked two (2); and G3 ranked three (3).\par
\par
City Manager Williams requested details regarding the Commission's evaluation criteria. City Attorney McCartney commented on evaluation criteria in State Statutes.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis remarked that with respect to qualifications, capabilities, and experience, all three (3) proposers were generally equal and what distinguished HPPP\rquote s proposal was its architectural design quality and the potential for revenue.\par
\par
Commissioner Glassman introduced this Resolution to proceed with Holiday Park Parking Partners LLC\rquote s proposal which was read by title only.\f1\par

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\f0\fs24 Mayor Trantalis recognized Ryan O'Connor, 2724 NE 15th Street. In response to Mayor Trantalis' question, Mr. O'Connor explained his concerns relate to insurance costs. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Milos Majstorovic, Transportation and Mobility (TAM) Department Director. Mr. Majstorovic explained that the City's $1,000,000 insurance requirement is based on guidance from the Risk Management Office and is intended to appropriately cover the elevated risk associated with these types of vehicles.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Guy Hine, Human Resources Department Risk Manager. Mr. Hine explained that the proposed $1,000,000 insurance requirement was based on both State Statute and prior City experience. Mr. Hine explained related information and cited a past incident that resulted in specific Commission direction. Further comment and discussion ensued regarding the travel volume of similar ride services.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Jose Barrios, 4161 SW 84th Terrace, Davie. Mr. Barrios spoke in support of regulating the industry, raised concerns about the high insurance coverage requirements, and confirmed the strain on small businesses. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Carlo Barrios, 1770 E. Las Olas Boulevard. Mr. Barrios reiterated concerns discussed regarding high insurance coverage requirements on small businesses and expounded on his viewpoint.\par
\par
In response to Mayor Trantalis' question, Mr. Majstorovic explained that the proposed ordinance relies primarily on permit fees and the potential suspension or revocation of a business license as enforcement tools, but it does not clearly articulate a direct monetary fine or strong financial disincentive for operating without a permit.\par
\par
In response to Mayor Trantalis' question, Morgan Dunn, Transportation and Mobility Department Program Manager, said that the existing ordinance imposes a $150 civil fine for operating without a required permit. \par
\par
Mayor Trantalis said a $150 fine was inadequate and stated that it provides little to no deterrent, suggesting that the penalty be increased to $1,000 to serve as a meaningful enforcement mechanism. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Commissioner Sorensen suggested that TAM staff meet with the operators to continue discussions. He confirmed his willingness to be involved in those discussions. \par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recommended deferring this Agenda item to refine the ordinance before moving forward. City Manager Williams confirmed this Agenda item would be deferred until the March 3, 2026, Commission Regular Meeting. Commissioner Glassman commented on the need to address this topic, cited examples of concerns, and discussed his viewpoint.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Paul Minoff, 110 SE 6th Street, on behalf of Cart Concierge, LLC. Mr. Minoff discussed his viewpoint regarding this Agenda item, expounded on related information and details, and cited examples.\par
\par
In response to Mayor Trantalis' question, Ms. Dunn explained that the existing ordinance lacks strong enforcement mechanisms, such as vehicle booting. Further comment and discussion ensued regarding interest in revisiting the regulatory framework to add more effective tools.\par
\par
Commissioner Beasley-Pittman expressed support for vehicle seizure as an enforcement mechanism, citing similar efforts to address illegal dirt bike activity. This approach is a more significant inconvenience and a more effective deterrent than modest fines or administrative penalties. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Commissioner Beasley-Pittman made a motion to defer this Ordinance on Second Reading to March 3, 2026, and was seconded by Commissioner Sorensen.\cf1\f1\par

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\sa160\sl276\slmult1\kerning2\f0\fs24 City Manager Williams provided opening remarks. \par
\par
Aricka Johnson, Structural Innovation Manager, Office of Management and Budget, moderated the meeting and narrated a presentation entitled \i CITY OF FORT LAUDERDALE VISION STRATEGY ACTION SETTING PRIORITIES FOR FY 2027\i0 that included a video.\par
\par
\b\i A copy of the presentation is part of the backup to this Agenda items. A copy of the video is available through the Office of the City Clerk.\par
\b0\i0\par
In response to Mayor Trantalis\rquote question, Ms. Johnson confirmed housing statistics listed in the presentation are applicable to the City, not Broward County.\par
\par
\ul Neighbor Surveys\par
\ulnone Mayor Trantalis discussed the interpretation of safety in context of its broad approach and expounded on his perspective. Ms. Johnson commented that safety is a holistic term, including home and community safety; financial safety; and natural disaster safety. Further comment and discussion ensued regarding those three (3) aspects of safety, survey insights, public safety concerns and recommendations.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis discussed the significant capital investment for infrastructure and remarked that community feedback could be based on perception, noting the need for improved community messaging and education. Further comment and discussion ensued. \par
\par
Commissioner Glassman concurred with Mayor Trantalis\rquote comments and emphasized the need to strengthen strategic communications and public education through improved messaging. City Manager Williams concurred and commented on staff efforts to redefine strategic communications. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis discussed homelessness concerns, acknowledged staff\rquote s significant efforts, and remarked on the perception of panhandling. He noted a primary barrier to solving homelessness is the lack of available affordable housing and that effective solutions require comprehensive wraparound services and continued proactive outreach. He noted the need to address public safety issues related to panhandling at busy intersections and urged the City\rquote s homeless outreach team to continue engaging those individuals. Mayor Trantalis suggested that nonprofit organizations serving the homeless improve their messaging to ensure individuals experiencing homelessness are aware of available resources. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Commissioner Sorensen discussed participating in a two-hour ride along on the newly launched\i Rotary Connect Bus\i0 , funded by the \i Rotary Club of Fort Lauderdale,\i0 that provides structured transportation for individuals experiencing homelessness and connecting them with essential service providers. Commissioner Sorensen expressed support for similar partnerships, recommended enhanced communications, and requested a monthly update on homelessness initiatives. City Manager Williams confirmed.\par
\par
Commissioner Glassman recommended enhanced collaboration between Strategic Communications and the Neighbor Support Division to ensure staff is consistently present at all neighborhood associations and Council of Fort Lauderdale Civic Association (CFLCA) meetings to provide cohesive and consistent messaging. Further comment and discussion ensued. City Manager Williams concurred.\par
\par
\ul Infrastructure\par
\ulnone Albert Carbon, Utility Services Department Director, presented an overview of opportunities related to inflow and infiltration (I&I) within the wastewater infrastructure system. The City is ahead of schedule in meeting requirements of the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) Consent Order and is proactively negotiating a second Consent Order amendment that will include a comprehensive I&I reduction component, and will be presented to the Commission in late spring. \par
\par
In response to Mayor Trantalis' question regarding what percentage of the I&I rehabilitation work that will be completed by March 2027, Mr. Carbon said that the original Consent Order requirement is to complete seventy-one (71) projects by March 2027. A second amendment provides an additional seven (7) year period to further mitigate I&I.\par
\par
\ul Broadband Access\par
\ulnone Ron McKenzie, Information Technology Services (ITS) Department Director, presented an overview of broadband access efforts, explaining key concepts and available service options. Mr. McKenzie explained that while broadband resources and affordability programs already exist, access gaps often stem from limited awareness, education, and infrastructure capacity. He outlined available broadband resources to residents and efforts to improve digital connectivity and equitable broadband access citywide.\par
\par
In response to Mayor Trantalis\rquote question regarding a potential expansion of surveillance cameras in crime hotspots, Mr. McKenzie said that staff is actively exploring options, commented on related funding, discussed the utilization of both broadband and Wi-Fi, and emphasized that image clarity and functionality are critical considerations. \par
\par
Mayor Trantalis confirmed his support for surveillance camera expansion with enhanced video coverage as an important public safety and accountability tool.\par
\par
City Manager Williams noted that the Commission approved a package that included additional camera equipment for Himmarshee Street and Sistrunk Boulevard. In response to Mayor Trantalis\rquote question, Mr. McKenzie provided an update on installation of that camera equipment and explained related information. Mayor Trantalis urged staff to expedite those efforts.\par
\par
Police Chief Bill Schultz said that existing cameras provided valuable footage for a recent investigation. The Police Department is coordinating with the ITS Department to advance deployment of four (4) new cameras that are expected to be operational by the end of the month, with the first installation site on Himmarshee Street. \par
\par
Commissioner Beasley-Pittman discussed her strong support for the proposed broadband enhancement initiatives, emphasizing the importance of workshops and training opportunities to assist District 3 residents who currently lack internet access. In response to Commissioner Beasley-Pittman\rquote s question regarding established timelines for executing related training sessions, Mr. McKenzie said staff is seeking Commission feedback on which enhancement options are most desirable before setting timelines and allocating resources. Multiple approaches could be pursued simultaneously, depending on the Commission\rquote s direction.\par
\par
Commissioner Sorensen concurred with Commissioner Beasley-Pittman\rquote s comments and recommended options B and C listed in the presentation. Commissioner Beasley-Pittman urged implementing all options. There was Commission consensus to support a comprehensive approach to broadband enhancement, including pilot program expansion, increased public bandwidth, resident training, and finalizing priorities and timelines to ensure effective implementation. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
\ul Fourth Police District\par
\ulnone Police Chief Schultz presented the proposal to create a Fourth (4th) Police District, which would focus on the downtown entertainment corridor. The focus and goals of the proposed Fourth (4th) Police District are to reorganize existing police staffing to improve response times, implement proactive policing without increasing overall personnel levels and would encompass approximately three (3) square miles. This configuration addresses operational challenges such as drawbridges and train crossings that can delay 911 response times.\par
\par
In response to Mayor Trantalis' question regarding whether creating a Fourth (4\super th\nosupersub ) Police District would involve hiring additional officers or reallocating existing personnel, Chief Schultz said that the proposal does not add new officers. It redistributes officers by shrinking portions of Districts 1 and 3 to form a new Fourth (4) Police District. \par
\par
Mayor Trantalis remarked on his understanding that the purpose of the proposed Fourth (4\super th\nosupersub ) Police District is to concentrate a designated number of officers within a smaller, more narrowly defined geographic area that experiences a higher volume of calls for service. Chief Schultz confirmed.\par
\par
In response to Mayor Trantalis\rquote question, Chief Schultz explained that inclusion of the Isles in the proposed Fourth (4\super th\nosupersub ) Police District is based on geographic response considerations related to drawbridge access and response logistics\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Sorensen's question regarding Police Districts mirroring Commission Districts, Chief Schultz said Police District boundaries are structured around operational and reporting considerations. The proposed Fourth (4\super th\nosupersub ) Police District prioritizes service, efficiency, and balance.\par
\par
Commissioner Glassman confirmed his support for the proposed Fourth (4\super th\nosupersub ) Police District and requested that the current police officer staffing levels on the barrier island remain. Chief Schultz confirmed, discussed current manpower levels, and noted that future police officer staffing figures will be determined in January 2027, based on contract cycles and overall staffing growth.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Beasley-Pittman\rquote s questions, Chief Schultz explained the Fourth (4\super th\nosupersub ) Police District would consist of approximately thirty (30) patrol officers and the other Districts would remain at thirty (30) to forty (40) officers. He reiterated that due to contractual restrictions, these changes will not take effect until January 2027. \par
\par
Mayor Trantalis expressed support for the Fourth (4\super th\nosupersub ) Police District, noting the need for a more concentrated police presence in that area and confirmed a Commission consensus that this is viable solution.\par
\par
\ul Old Federal Courthouse\par
\ulnone Ben Rogers, Assistant City Manager, discussed the Government Services Administration Office (GSA) disposal process for the old Federal Courthouse (OFC) and reviewed details and options for its Public Benefit Conveyance (PBC). Mayor Trantalis suggested establishing a charter school focused on artificial intelligence education at the OFC and discussed related information.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Beasley-Pittman's question regarding how historic designation of the OFC could affect the City\rquote s PBC option, Mr. Rogers explained that historic designation is still undergoing federal review, and the City does not yet know what restricted covenants or use limitations may be imposed. Mr. Rogers explained details of GSA\rquote s process and said that the City will not know the related restrictions until it formally submits an offer to GSA. Further comment and discussion ensued regarding restricted covenants and the difficulty of evaluating conveyance options for future use of the property. \par
\par
Mr. Rogers noted the most significant issue associated with historic designation is the concept of \ldblquote adverse action\rdblquote and explained that if the City significantly alters the building, federal preservation rules could require mitigation measures to address impacts on the structure\rquote s historic value. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Glassman\rquote s question, Mr. Rogers confirmed that GSA has begun evaluating the OFC property for potential listing on the National Register of Historic Places (National Register) as part of its preparation for future disposal. \par
\par
Commissioner Glassman discussed his understanding of the OFC\rquote s National Register designation, which would recognize its historic significance but likely impose fewer regulatory constraints than local historic designation and remarked on related information. Commissioner Glassman expanded on his perspective and the historical significance of the OFC property. He recommended putting a placeholder on the property for use as an educational venue. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis remarked on possible educational opportunities with Florida Atlantic University. Commissioner Glassman commented on the interest of other entities in the OFC.\par
\par
Chris Cooper, Deputy City Manager, provided clarification regarding historic preservation considerations. Local historic designation would impose stricter preservation standards than national and state designation but would not prevent redevelopment or adaptive reuse of the OFC. \par
\par
Mayor Trantalis said that the GSA is seeking clarity on a preferred eligible public use to begin evaluating a potential PBC, which could allow transfer of the OFC at a substantial discount. Further comment and discussion ensued. Mayor Trantalis recommended focusing on educational use.\par
\par
Commissioner Sorensen suggested using the property as affordable housing. Mayor Trantalis remarked on related high conversion costs. Commissioner Sorensen discussed partnering with developers, noting the large amount of infrastructure challenges. Further comment and discussion ensued. \par
\par
Commissioner Glassman remarked on challenges related to converting this historically designated property to residential affordable housing.\par
\par
Commissioner Glassman said that he had been meeting with potential partners to explore possible OFC redevelopment concepts, particularly those involving education, which include combining the OFC with adjacent vacant land that could improve financial viability, attract investment, and create a stronger redevelopment opportunity.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Beasley-Pittman's question regarding the meaning of a \ldblquote 100% discount\rdblquote under the GSA\rquote s PBC process, Mr. Rogers confirmed that the OFC could be conveyed to the City at no purchase cost, provided the City selects and qualifies under an approved public-use. Further comment and discussion ensued regarding the importance of identifying multiple eligible uses for the OFC, including education, affordable housing, and recreational use. Mayor Trantalis confirmed a consensus to focus on education or affordable housing options. Mr. Rogers confirmed that staff would present both education and affordable housing as PBC options to the GSA.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Sorensen\rquote s question, Mayor Trantalis said that the City does not have the financial resources for a negotiated sale of the OFC. \par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recessed the meeting at 10:54 a.m.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis reconvened the meeting at 11:07 a.m.\par
\par
\ul One Stop Shop\par
\ulnone Chris Cooper, Deputy City Manager, presented a brief historical overview of the One Stop Shop site (Site). Mr. Cooper requested Commission guidance on potential next steps to determine the preferred long-term vision for the Site.\par
\par
Commissioner Glassman remarked on resident feedback regarding the Site\rquote s future use, which included keeping it culturally oriented open green space without overdevelopment. Commissioner Glassman noted growing interest from community organizations and local agencies to participate in planning and activation of the Site, including entities involved with Huizenga Park initiatives. \par
\par
Commissioner Glassman asked staff to provide guidance on the merits of City-led development versus partnerships with private or institutional partners experienced in managing similar public spaces.\par
\par
Commissioner Beasley-Pittman commented on her support for obtaining community input regarding the future use of the Site and reiterated her preference for preserving significant green space and avoiding overdevelopment. She indicated openness to revisiting concepts like the previously proposed project, provided the design maintains a strong open-space component. \par
\par
Commissioner Sorensen confirmed his support for keeping the Site as open park green space.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis discussed the success of nearby Flagler Village as a residential district and emphasized that its long-term sustainability depends on adding activated public spaces and amenities. Further comment and discussion ensued regarding the next step to solicit redevelopment concepts for the Site.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis provided direction to staff that the City should invite unsolicited proposals to identify creative ways to activate the Site and prioritize maintaining significant open space while adding functional, programmed uses that make the property an active public asset versus a passive park.\par
\par
City Manager Williams noted that the Site is being considered a suitable location for needed sewer lift station infrastructure to sustain continued downtown development. Mr. Cooper explained related details and noted that the Site is an ideal location. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
City Manager Williams summarized Commission feedback, noting direction to activate the Site as primarily green space and public park land, while also exploring opportunities for a public-private partnership (P3) to support development and long-term operations. Further comment and discussion ensued regarding pursuing a solicited P3 process that establishes a defined framework and baseline requirements. Commissioner Glassman discussed his support for this approach, noting that past unsolicited proposal processes often evolved into projects resembling solicited procurements or design-build projects.\par
\par
In response to Mayor Trantalis\rquote question, City Manager Williams explained that a solicited P3 would function as a structured partnership where the City sets required project elements upfront, allowing developers flexibility to propose creative solutions that will streamline decision-making. City Manager Williams said that staff will explore potential external partners to manage and operate the Site in coordination with the Office of the City Attorney to ensure legal compliance.\par
\par
\ul New City Hall\par
\ulnone Yvette Matthews, Assistant City Manager, provided an update on financing for the proposed new City Hall project (Project). In response to Mayor Trantalis' question, City Manager Williams said preliminary indications suggest the Project could be delivered within a $200,000,000 budget.\par
\par
In response to Mayor Trantalis' question, Ms. Matthews confirmed the City received $88,000,000 in Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) funding as a result of the April 2023 flood. \par
\par
In response to Mayor Trantalis' question regarding what portion of the FEMA funding could be used for the Project, Mr. Cooper explained Community Development Block Grant Disaster Recovery (CDBG-DR) funding may provide limited support for eligible Project components due to federal rules and timing constraints. City Manager Williams explained staff efforts to determine availability and use of CDBG-DR funds for components of the Project. Mayor Trantalis remarked on his initial understanding regarding the use of FEMA funding. In response to Mayor Trantalis\rquote question, Ms. Matthews confirmed FEMA funds were used for demolition costs of the old City Hall. In response to Mayor Trantalis\rquote question, City Manager Williams said there would be a robust effort to keep the Commission and the community updated on the Project. Mr. Rogers noted that the goal is to present a term sheet to the Commission for review and approval at the first Commission meeting in March. Based on Commission feedback on the term sheet, an interim agreement would be developed and brought forward. \par
\par
Commissioner Glassman expressed concern about the pace of the schedule. In response to Commissioner Glassman\rquote s question regarding the results of the first meeting with Fort Lauderdale City Hall Partners, City Manager Williams said it was positive. City Attorney McCartney concurred and expounded on related information and confirmed efforts to move forward as quickly as possible.\par
\par
Commissioner Sorensen remarked on the Project\rquote s $200,000,000 target budget. Mayor Trantalis commented on his perspective regarding that amount being a realistic cost. Further comment and discussion ensued. Commissioner Glassman noted the need to prioritize a realistic scope and long-term planning approach to minimize costly change orders caused by underestimating needs during early planning stages.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recessed the meeting at 11:40 a.m.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis reconvened the meeting at 12:24 p.m.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Marilyn Mammano, on behalf of \i Lauderdale Tomorrow. \i0 Ms. Mammano read from a prepared statement discussing City priorities.\par
\par
\b\i A copy of the document has been attached to these Meeting Minutes. \par
\b0\i0\par
In response to Commissioner Sorensen\rquote s question, staff confirmed $27,000,000 in traffic improvement funding. \par
\par
Mayor Trantalis noted that the current P3 process is working. Further comment and discussion ensued regarding priorities related to homelessness program evaluation, and expanding green space.\par
\par
\ul District 2\par
\ulnone Commissioner Glassman discussed feedback from District 2 residents and said that the City\rquote s existing goals and priorities remain broadly aligned with residents\rquote concerns and expounded on his viewpoint. He said that neighborhood specific concerns would be shared separately with the City Manager\rquote s Office for follow-up.\par
\par
Commissioner Glassman remarked on overall concerns expressed by residents that include the need for improved community area restoration practices by Florida Power & Light (FPL), citing examples and recommendations. Additional resident concerns include flood mitigation and infrastructure improvements, illegal dumping in waterways, and the need for better regulation of marine pump-out facilities. He noted the need for increased emphasis on parking enforcement, traffic management, and delivery trucks obstructing traffic along State Road A1A. District 2 residents requested continued focus on the impact from king tides and heavy rainfall events, accelerating seawall improvement projects, addressing traffic congestion and public safety concerns related to electric bikes (e-bikes) and scooters.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Glassman's question regarding neighbor concerns about e-bikes and similar electric devices, Chief Schultz discussed enforcement challenges, police engagement, and said that e-bikes are largely governed by State law, limiting local regulation. Chief Schultz noted efforts with the Office of the City Attorney to address related concerns and confirmed that the Police Department is actively enforcing violations. Chief Schultz said that he will pursue legislative changes at the State level during Broward Days.\par
\par
Commissioner Glassman summarized feedback from District 2 neighborhoods that largely align with the City\rquote s existing priorities that include mobility improvements, enhanced street lighting and public safety measures, infrastructure projects, and continued investment in public spaces. Residents are seeking faster implementation rather than new initiatives. He remarked that similar priorities were reflected in feedback from the Downtown Development Authority (DDA), while Riverwalk representatives emphasized concerns about the slow pace of seawall replacement along the New River. Commissioner Glassman noted positive resident feedback regarding recent improvements to roadway medians and overall landscaping aesthetics.\par
\ul\par
District 3\par
\ulnone Commissioner Beasley-Pittman said that the City\rquote s existing priorities are aligned with community goals but recommended expanding efforts in several key areas, particularly public safety and infrastructure. \par
\par
Commissioner Beasley-Pittman highlighted the Police Department\rquote s recent \i Gun Violence Interruption Pilot Program\i0 , a community-based public safety initiative developed in partnership with John Jay College, and recommended that this initiative be included in long-term funding and expansion plans.\par
\par
Commissioner Beasley-Pittman discussed concerns regarding aging underground pipes in District 3, particularly in areas such as Lake Aire and Rock Island, where roadway depressions and sinkhole-like conditions are occurring. She urged a more proactive and comprehensive evaluation of underground infrastructure.\par
\par
Brad Kaine, Public Works Department Director, acknowledged those concerns and committed to further evaluation, coordination across departments, and prioritization of roadway, sidewalk, and infrastructure improvements using available bond funding and remarked on related challenges and details. \par
\par
Commissioner Beasley-Pittman encouraged a proactive, coordinated approach to infrastructure projects to ensure timely, comprehensive roadway repairs. She reiterated support for maintaining current City priorities while strengthening community-based public safety programs and adopting a more proactive, coordinated strategy to address aging infrastructure.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis discussed similar infrastructure concerns along NE 18th Street in Poinsettia Heights, where a major sewer pipe installation caused sinkholes and roadway depressions, creating ongoing maintenance and safety concerns. Mr. Kaine acknowledged that issue and committed to reviewing the conditions and investigating the cause of the recurring roadway failures. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Commissioner Beasley-Pittman proposed expanding public safety initiatives to include a swimming proficiency program, emphasizing the importance of water safety. She expounded on the need to ensure that every child learns not only basic water survival skills but also how to swim proficiently enough to protect themselves in emergency situations. Further comment and discussion ensued regarding pursuing this initiative, including partnering with the International Swimming Hall of Fame, the YMCA, and other existing aquatic facilities to ensure expansion of youth swimming programs as part of a broader public safety initiative. Further comment and discussion ensued regarding support for expanding water safety programming.\par
\par
In response to Mayor Trantalis\rquote question, Carl Williams, Parks and Recreation Department Director, provided an overview of existing swim instruction and aquatic programs. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis encouraged staff to explore ways to promote and ensure swimming instruction is accessible and appealing to young residents, including increased outreach, expansion, and programming with existing aquatic facilities to promote this initiative. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Commissioner Beasley-Pittman emphasized the importance of the City\rquote s continued commitment to economic growth and entrepreneurship, her support of continued investment in programs like \i Startup Fort Lauderdale\i0 and expounded on her perspective. City Manager Williams discussed the updated organizational structure and recruitment efforts to fill the Chief Economic Development Officer position.\par
\par
\ul District 4\par
\ulnone Commissioner Sorensen expressed confidence regarding efforts across major focus areas, including infrastructure, public safety, quality of life, and affordability.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Sorensen\rquote s questions regarding an update on the Riverwalk seawall replacement project (RSR Project), Mr. Kaine explained that the RSR Project is advancing after previous delays due to permitting and commented on related details. Staff is pursuing funding strategies that include grants to close a $4,000,000 funding gap. Mr. Rogers explained that the RSR Project extends from Andrews Avenue to the Florida East Coast Railroad tracks and is continuing through the design phase. Mr. Rogers confirmed pursuing a Florida Inland Navigation District (FIND) grant to close the $4,000,000 funding gap and expounded on related information.\par
\par
Commissioner Sorensen remarked on the poor condition of the Riverwalk Seawall, cited examples, and remarked on aesthetic concerns. Mr. Rogers noted securing a $1,000,000 FIND grant last year for upland improvements and staff is exploring how those funds can be used to address Riverwalk Seawall needs until full funding for the RSR Project is determined.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Sorensen\rquote s request for an overview of funding for the Las Olas Mobility Project (LOM Project), Milos Majstorovic, Transportation and Mobility Department Director, provided an update and explained that the City will present the LOM Project at a future Commission meeting, followed by a request for Commission direction on the preferred design option for the Retail Shops segment. Construction costs for the Retail Shops segment are estimated at approximately $7,500,000, and improvements across the entire western corridor extending from Andrews Avenue to Southeast 17th Avenue are estimated to be $19,300,000. Further comment and discussion ensued regarding multiple funding sources and the funding gap.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis emphasized the need for a fact-based discussion regarding the future and longevity of the median trees in the Retail Shops segment. He referenced information from the City\rquote s urban forester indicating that the median trees have an estimated life expectancy of approximately eight (8) to twelve (12) years. Mr. Majstorovic said there would be an upcoming Commission Conference Meeting presentation to support an informed decision. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Sorensen\rquote s question regarding the LOM Project funding gap, City Manager Williams said funding will depend on Commission priorities from multiple sources and, if directed by the Commission, general fund allocations.\par

\par
Mayor Trantalis opened the public hearing.\par
\par
\cf0 In response to Vice Mayor Herbst's question regarding the lack of a letter of support from the neighboring building, Stephanie Toothaker, Esq., 901 Ponce de Leon Drive, on behalf of the Applicant, explained related outreach that did not result in a letter of support. Ms. Toothaker clarified that neighboring Nola Lofts condominium owners were aware of the planned development, as purchasers signed documents at the time of sale acknowledging that future development would occur as part of Phase II, and expounded on related details.\par
\cf1\par
There being no one else wishing to speak on this item, Vice Mayor Herbst made a motion to close the public hearing, and was seconded by Commissioner Sorensen. Roll call showed AYES: Vice Mayor Herbst, Commissioner Glassman, Commissioner Beasley-Pittman, Commissioner Sorensen, and Mayor Trantalis.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Anthony Fajardo, Development Services Department Director. Mr. Fajardo noted that Approval Condition No. 3 should be removed, as it is not applicable and the agreement does not need to be recorded.\par
\par
Commissioner Glassman introduced this Resolution as amended excluding Condition No. 3 which was read by title only.\par

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\sa160\kerning2\fs24 Mayor Trantalis recognized Ellyn Bogdanoff, One E. Broward Boulevard, on behalf of Tachers, Appellant. Ms. Bogdanoff explained details of this matter. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
\pard\sa160\tx720 Mayor Trantalis recognized Selena Gibson, Esq., Board of Adjustment (BOA) Counsel. Ms. Gibson said that the BOA acted properly and that the Commission should uphold the BOA\rquote s decision. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
In response to Mayor Trantalis\rquote question, Ms. Gibson explained that to obtain a variance, applicants must prove a unique hardship not created by themselves or prior owners. Further comment and discussion ensued. \par
\par
In response to Mayor Trantalis\rquote question, Anthony Fajardo, Development Services Department Director, said that the Code does not automatically grandfather old variance permit violations and said that legal court case precedents could be relevant. Mayor Trantalis remarked on his perspective. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Commissioner Sorensen discussed his understanding of this matter and the process. The shed was built under a City issued permit and the permit was closed, indicating the construction was completed and approved by the City. Mr. Fajardo confirmed. Ms. Gibson explained the permit dimensions were exceeded, and staff closed the permit without realizing that discrepancy. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
In response to Mayor Trantalis\rquote questions, Mr. Fajardo noted issues related to this matter include shed dimensions and remarked on zoning setbacks and building separation.\par
\par
Commissioner Sorensen said that because the City issued and closed the permit, the new homeowner likely assumed the structure was compliant. He said that requiring correction now would impose an unfair hardship on the current owner.\par
\par
Ms. Gibson explained this appeal is limited to two legal standards: determining whether the BOA departed from the essential requirements of the law and whether its decision was supported by competent, substantial evidence. Ms. Gibson noted that the BOA thoroughly considered the matter, holding an extensive discussion before voting 3-2, noting that the motion ultimately failed because it did not achieve the required majority plus one vote. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\pard\sa160\par
Commissioner Sorensen made a motion to extend this meeting until 12:00 a.m. and was seconded by Commissioner Beasley-Pittman.\par
\par
\b APPROVED\par
Yea\b0 : 5 - Vice Mayor Herbst , Commissioner Glassman, Commissioner Beasley-Pittman, Commissioner Sorensen, and Mayor Trantalis\par
\pard\sa160\tx720\par
Commissioner Glassman said the BOA\rquote s decision lacked competent, substantial evidence. Mayor Trantalis concurred, expounded on his viewpoint, and said a final Commission decision could be made at a de novo hearing. Further comment and discussion ensued regarding the BOA\rquote s decision.\par
\par
In response to City Attorney McCartney\rquote s question, Commissioner Sorensen clarified the basis for setting the de novo hearing is due to the BOA\rquote s departure from the essential elements of law.\par
\pard\sa160\par
There being no one else wishing to speak on this item, Commissioner Sorensen made a motion to close the public hearing and was seconded by Commissioner Glassman. Roll call showed AYES: Vice Mayor Herbst, Commissioner Glassman, Commissioner Beasley-Pittman, Commissioner Sorensen, and Mayor Trantalis.\par
\pard\sa160\tx720\par
Commissioner Sorensen introduced a Resolution to set a de novo hearing on February 17, 2026, based on competent and substantial evidence not existing to support the BOA\rquote s decision.\par
}
