\viewkind4\uc1\pard\sa160\kerning2\fs24 Mayor Trantalis opened the public hearing.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Chris Cooper, Deputy City Manager. Mr. Cooper provided an overview of this Agenda item. In response Mayor Trantalis' question, Mr. Cooper confirmed that this Ordinance would prohibit the outdoor sale and consumption of alcoholic beverages, except at licensed and permitted outdoor caf\'e9s, and would update the hours permitted to sell and serve alcoholic beverages within Special Entertainment Districts (SED). Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
In response to Vice Mayor Herbst's questions, Mr. Cooper provided background information regarding the establishment of SEDs and explained their locations and geographic boundaries. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Glassman's question, Mr. Cooper explained a minor scrivener's error in the heading of this Agenda item.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Ellyn Bogdanoff, Esq., One E. Broward Boulevard, on behalf of Sway and other bar owners in the Himmarshee Special Entertainment District (HSED). Ms. Bogdanoff acknowledged past shortcomings in self-regulation among HSED business operators and expressed the group\rquote s willingness to improve oversight. She stated that these businesses are presenting a unified position in seeking a reasonable compromise regarding aspects of this Ordinance affecting their business operations.\par
\par
In response to Mayor Trantalis\rquote questions, Ms. Bogdanoff clarified that the affected businesses are willing to discontinue outdoor alcoholic beverage sales and consumption unless specifically licensed. She confirmed their only remaining concern is the proposed change to alcoholic beverage sales and service hours, as they wish to maintain the current hours. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
In response to Mayor Trantalis' question, Ms. Bogdanoff explained proposed enforcement and security options that would be paid for by the bar owners and cited examples. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis said that Ordinance changes stem from recent incidents in the HSED and Beach Place SED, emphasizing that public safety concerns require the City to act. He noted that certain aspects of SEDs such as outdoor alcohol sales and extended 4:00 a.m. closing hours may contribute to an environment that encourages those types of incidents. The Commission is considering restricting outdoor sales and reducing weekend hours by one (1) hour to discourage late-night disturbances and prevent further public safety incidents. Further comment and discussion ensued. \par
\par
Mr. Cooper discussed staff efforts to address HSED public safety concerns and expounded on related information.\par
\par
Commissioner Glassman said that multiple parallel discussions and planning efforts have not resulted in concrete action, emphasizing the need to implement change, and expounded on his viewpoint.\par
\par
Commissioner Sorensen suggested immediate action to prohibit open container and outdoor alcohol sales, while allowing a short, defined window for further collaboration on broader oversight measures to ensure new rules are in place before Spring Break.\par
\par
City Attorney McCartney advised against combining multiple issues into a single ordinance action, recommended a phased approach, and expounded on related recommendations and details.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis emphasized the need for urgency, stating that measurable public safety supervisory improvements must be in place by the second meeting in February 2026 and prior to Spring Break. If voluntary agreements and meaningful security commitments are not demonstrated by bar operators within that timeframe, the Commission could proceed with formal Ordinance changes, including potential adjustments to hours of operation.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Herbst said that the problems in the HSED are longstanding and that some operators have a poor track record of self-policing, and expounded on specific behavior that must cease. If operators fail to properly regulate their establishments, the City will intervene with stricter enforcement or regulatory action. Vice Mayor Herbst expounded his viewpoint regarding the need to eliminate open containers and reiterated that businesses must take responsibility for improving conditions within their establishments. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis said that the City should not bear the sole burden of maintaining public safety within the HSED. He indicated his willingness to move forward with the Ordinance but removing the proposed change to hours of operation on weekends. Mayor Trantalis emphasized that this approach would rely on operators within the HSED to organize collectively and participate, including funding a voluntary program to ensure enhanced public safety law enforcement measures. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Commissioner Glassman discussed conditions in the HSED, including underage drinking, safety concerns, and deteriorating aesthetics such as cleanliness and maintenance that have not improved despite prior commitments from operators. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Commissioner Glassman emphasized that businesses benefiting from SED designation must adhere to the agreement governing the SED, and that enforcement actions should not affect other SEDs that are operating responsibly. Further comment and discussion ensued. \par
\par
Commissioner Sorensen indicated a willingness to proceed with restrictions on open containers and outdoor alcohol sales without altering hours but said that if operating hours are to be debated, the Commission should continue this conversation. Commissioner Glassman concurred. Mayor Trantalis noted a decision regarding hours of operation had not been made and confirmed a consensus on the other topics that would be included in the Ordinance on the Second Reading. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis said hours of SED operations would proceed to public comment. Commissioner Glassman requested clearer alignment on the agreed process. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Richard Mercede, 327 SW 2nd Street. Mr. Mercede spoke in support of the proposed ordinance modifications including modifying HSED hours of operation. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Steve Berke, 200 SW 2nd Street. Mr. Berke spoke in opposition to modifying the HSED hours of operation. In response to Vice Mayor Herbst\rquote s question regarding whether extended hours contribute to disorder and the City\rquote s party reputation, Mr. Berke said that nightlife is part of Fort Lauderdale\rquote s identity and stronger enforcement of outdoor drinking rules would resolve most problems without harming businesses. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Glassman's question as to why businesses not formally part of the HSED appear to be operating with SED privileges, Mr. Cooper discussed related information and noted decisions must be made to formally incorporate those establishments into a restructured HSED framework or enforce existing code provisions to restrict those privileges. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Commissioner Beasley-Pittman noted that the Ordinance under discussion would apply citywide, affecting all five (5) SEDs, and cautioned that the Commission should consider the impact on those SEDs that are operating responsibly. \par
\par
In response to Mayor Trantalis\rquote question, Mr. Cooper explained details and information associated with the five (5) SEDs. Mayor Trantalis acknowledged that the former governance structure for the HSED had dissolved, yet businesses continue to operate as if it remains in place, highlighting the need for the City to formally update and clarify their regulatory framework. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Sorensen\rquote s questions, City Attorney McCartney confirmed that a common control entity does not exist in the HSED. Mr. Cooper said that the current governance framework for the HSED is largely ineffective due to the collapse of the original common control structure, but it technically remains in effect for certain businesses until the Commission either decertifies the HSED or adopts a revised Ordinance establishing a new regulatory structure. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Commissioner Sorensen noted that the original eight (8) businesses covered under the HSED common control agreement are authorized for extended hours and said all others should follow standard alcohol service hours until the Commission formally revises HSED policy framework to allow additional establishments to formally join. Mayor Trantalis said that would be a separate discussion.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Larry Mele, 327 SW 2nd Street. Mr. Mele discussed his viewpoint regarding this Agenda item and related safety concerns.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Danny Colica, 307 SW 2nd Street, Chemistry Night Club. Mr. Colica spoke in opposition to this Agenda item.\par
\par
In response to Mayor Trantalis\rquote question, City Attorney McCartney confirmed that underage drinking is illegal on City streets. Further comment and discussion ensued regarding related enforcement and regulatory measures within SEDs.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Jayme Norris-Kinghorn, Plantation. Ms. Norris-Kinghorn discussed her opposition to this Agenda item. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Herbst discussed legal and enforcement limitations related to open container laws and age identification documents that highlight the need to revise the Ordinance.\par
\par
City Attorney McCartney acknowledged enforcement challenges, noting that the current structure of the Ordinance creates inconsistency, which complicates uniform enforcement, and expounded on her viewpoint regarding Ordinance revisions. Further comment and discussion ensued regarding the alcohol service hours.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis stated that a clear pathway should exist for businesses to operate during later hours and noted the SEDs were originally created as an experimental policy to cluster nightlife venues and promote economic development. The City must now reassess and make related determinations and establish a clear policy framework for potential late-night operations.\par
\par
Commissioner Glassman discussed the possibility of allowing limited extended alcohol service hours for holidays or special events as part of a SED policy. City Manager Williams confirmed staff would explore that option. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Derrick Kurzrok. Mr. Kurzrok spoke in opposition to this Agenda item.\par
\par
Commissioner Sorensen made a motion to extend this meeting until 11:00 p.m. and was seconded by Vice Mayor Herbst.\par
\par
\b APPROVED\par
\par
Yea\b0 : 5 - Vice Mayor Herbst, Commissioner Glassman, Commissioner Beasley-Pittman, Commissioner Sorensen, and Mayor Trantalis\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Marc Dickerman, 1417 SW 2nd Street. Mr. Dickerman spoke in support of this Agenda item.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Tim Petrillo, 221 S. Andrews Avenue. Mr. Petrillo discussed his perspective regarding this Agenda item.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized William Brown, 112 N. Birch Road, and Central Beach Alliance (CBA) President. Mr. Brown spoke in support of this Agenda item, stating community leaders expressed support for stronger regulation and enforcement in SEDs, citing public safety concerns and the strain placed on limited police resources.\par
\par
\pard Mayor Trantalis recognized Dev Motwani, 2415 Delmar Place. Mr. Motwani discussed his viewpoint and recommended\cf1\kerning0 a tailored, district-specific approach with stakeholder engagement to mitigate business impacts. \cf0\kerning2 Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\pard\sa160\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Sandy Fey, 211 SW 2nd Street, on behalf of Riverwalk Center, Ltd. Mr. Fey spoke in opposition to this Agenda item.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Eric Magid, 211 SW 2nd Street, on behalf of Riverwalk Center, Ltd. Mr. Magid spoke in opposition to this Agenda item.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Sorensen\rquote s question, Police Chief William Schultz said that Police Officers are actively enforcing laws in the HSED, encouraged residents to report related enforcement concerns, and discussed results of a recent enforcement initiative. \par
\par
In response to Commissioner Sorensen's questions, Chief Schultz explained that while recreational marijuana is illegal in Florida, officers must have reasonable suspicion before requesting identification or taking enforcement action. Chief Schultz confirmed that calls for service are higher in the HSED compared to other SEDs and explained related details.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Glassman\rquote s questions regarding activity in downtown parking garages, Chief Schultz said increased police presence in public garages has reduced complaints, while enforcement in private garages depends on paid police details. Since implementing a recent action plan and increasing patrols, the department has not received additional complaints regarding activity in the City garages.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Sorensen\rquote s questions, Fire-Rescue Chief Stephen Gollan reported that late-night activity in the HSED significantly increases emergency calls, especially between midnight and 4:00 a.m., which strains Fire-Rescue resources and diverts units from responding to other city emergencies. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Ian Lowe, 320 SW 2nd Street, on behalf of Original Fat Cats. Mr. Lowe spoke in opposition to reducing late night hours in the HSED. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Sorensen\rquote s questions, Mr. Cooper explained that participation in SED common control agreements change over time as businesses entered or exited the district and explained related information.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Sorensen\rquote s question, City Attorney McCartney explained that any regulatory changes to SED rules must be applied uniformly citywide unless the Commission formally pursues the legal process to decertify a specific district and expounded on related information. Further comment and discussion ensued\par
\par
In response to Vice Mayor Herbst\rquote s question regarding the breakdown of late-night sales and whether food versus alcohol sales could be separated if alcohol service ended earlier, Mr. Lowe stated that 32% of his total monthly revenue occurs between 2:00 a.m. and 4:00 a.m., and did not have a specific breakdown between food and beverage sales. Vice Mayor Herbst suggested the option of ending alcohol service at 3:00 a.m., while allowing businesses to remain open until 4:00 a.m. Mr. Lowe explained the late-night hours are essential to his business, which primarily serve hospitality workers finishing their shifts.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Chanel Cowart, 2015 SW 2nd Street, on behalf of Ebar Club 13. Ms. Cowart discussed her viewpoint regarding this Agenda item and expounded on related information. \par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Samantha Costlow, 220 NW 2nd Street. Ms. Costlow spoke in opposition to this Agenda item. Further comment and discussion ensued. In response to Commissioner Sorensen\rquote s questions, Ms. Costlow explained off-shift customer business and discussed related information.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognied Samy Guerrero, 5500 Harrison Street, Hollywood, on behalf of Fat Tuesday. Mr. Guerrero discussed his viewpoint regarding this Agenda item.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Richard Coker, 1133 SE 4th Avenue, on behalf of Dicey Riley. Mr. Coker spoke in opposition to this Agenda item. In response to Commissioner Sorensen\rquote s question, Mr. Coker confirmed underage drinking is an issue in the HSED.\par
\par
There being no one else wishing to speak on this item, Commissioner Sorensen made a motion to close the public hearing, and was seconded by Commissioner Beasley-Pittman. Roll call showed AYES: Vice Mayor Herbst, Commissioner Glassman, Commissioner Beasley-Pittman, Commissioner Sorensen, and Mayor Trantalis.\par
\par
Commissioner Sorensen made a motion to extend this meeting until 11:30 p.m. and was seconded by Vice Mayor Herbst.\par
\par
\b APPROVED\par
\par
Yea: \b0 5 - Vice Mayor Herbst, Commissioner Glassman, Commissioner Beasley-Pittman, Commissioner Sorensen, and Mayor Trantalis\par
\par
Commissioner Glassman recommended taking incremental steps by immediately addressing issues with open containers and outdoor alcohol sales while delaying decisions regarding late-night closing hours. Business stakeholders should be allowed additional time to collaborate on solutions and compliance. Commissioner Glassman suggested revisiting the issue prior to Spring Break to evaluate progress and determine whether additional regulatory changes are necessary.\par
\par
In response to Mayor Trantalis\rquote question, Commissioner Glassman introduced the Ordinance to move forward with restrictions on open containers and outdoor alcohol sales while keeping the current operating hours.\par
\par
Commissioner Sorensen discussed the possibility of creating a future permitting process that would allow certain businesses to operate until 4:00 a.m. on a case-by-case or event-by-event basis. City Attorney McCartney explained what developing such a framework would require and cited examples that would extend beyond Spring Break.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Sorensen\rquote s questions, City Manager Williams clarified the current regulatory structure in the HSED. Six (6) businesses are parties to the original agreement and are permitted to operate until 4:00 a.m. along with additional privileges that she cited. All other businesses are required to comply with Code. \par
\par
Commissioner Sorensen discussed concerns related to establishments operating as if they are part of the HSED, inconsistent enforcement and the City\rquote s role in allowing the situation to continue for years. Further comment and discussion ensued regarding structural problems with the HSED framework, not having a governing entity, and the need for a comprehensive ordinance overhaul.\par
\par
Commissioner Glassman raised concerns that the City has allowed businesses in this area to operate beyond Code limits for years and expounded on his viewpoint. Further comment and discussion ensued regarding creating a process for extended hours of operation. \par
\par
Mayor Trantalis expounded on his perspective regarding allowing additional businesses to operate until 4:00 a.m. if they agree to meet the same requirements as the six (6) establishments authorized under the HSED agreement. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
City Attorney McCartney explained that the original common control entity governing HSED membership no long exists. Without a common control entity there is no formal mechanism for businesses to join or leave the district.\par
\par
Commissioner Glassman discussed his viewpoint that inconsistent enforcement over the years has contributed to the current issues. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Commissioner Sorensen emphasized the need for stronger enforcement and stated that the City should immediately implement new rules prohibiting open containers and on-street alcohol sales and expounded on his perspective. Further comment and discussion ensued regarding delaying decisions on reduced hours of operation and giving staff approximately ninety (90) days to develop a comprehensive enforcement and regulatory framework.\par
\par
Commissioner Sorensen discussed whether a SED framework would be necessary if businesses individually applied for extended operating hours. City Attorney McCartney explained that the district could remain geographically defined while replacing the current common control system with a permit-based process if they meet specific criteria. Maintaining district boundaries would limit where these privileges apply and allow enforcement compliance on an individual basis.\v \v0\par
\par
Vice Mayor Herbst confirmed his support for banning open containers and on-street alcohol sales and agreed to test the policy for six (6) months before reconsidering additional measures.\par
\par
Commissioner Beasley-Pittman stated that she supports the Ordinance as amended and agreed with the comments previously expressed by Commission Members.\par
\par
In response to City Clerk Soloman\rquote s question, City Attorney McCartney clarified details related to Commissioner Glassman\rquote s introduction of this Ordinance.\par
\par
In response to Mayor Trantalis\rquote question, City Manager Williams explained aspects of the Ordinance updates between First and Second Reading.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Sorensen\rquote s question, Mayor Trantalis confirmed that the open container and on-street alcohol sales bans will apply to all SEDs throughout the City.\par
\par
Commissioner Glassman introduced this Ordinance which was read by title only.\cf1\kerning0\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\fs24 Mayor Trantalis recognized Courtney Crush, Crush Law, on behalf of the applicant. Ms. Crush explained her viewpoint that the Historic Preservation Board's (HPB) denial of a certificate of appropriateness related to the installation of artificial turf in front of the building was based on incorrect historical assumptions and misapplied review criteria.\par
\par
In response to Mayor Trantalis' question regarding the purpose and benefits of installing artificial turf, Ms. Crush explained that it would enhance the appearance of the space and create a more comfortable walking surface compared to the existing pavers.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Esthel Brennan, 732 SW 13th Avenue. Ms. Brennan discussed concerns regarding artificial turf.\par
\par
In response to Vice Mayor Herbst's question, City Attorney McCartney discussed pending State legislation that may preempt local regulation of artificial turf and recommended monitoring the outcome before making policy decisions. Deputy City Manager Chris Cooper provided additional information.\par
\par
\cf0 Mayor Trantalis recognized William Brown, 112 N. Birch Road, and Central Beach Alliance (CBA) President. Mr. Brown said the CBA does not have an issue with the artificial turf and spoke in support of setting a De Novo Hearing.\par
\par
In response to Mayor Trantalis' question regarding whether the HPB had extended its authority beyond the historically designated fa\'e7ade area by evaluating the turf installation, City Attorney McCartney clarified that the historic protection applies to the fa\'e7ade. The HPB reviewed the artificial turf installation on the basis that it could visually impact the protected fa\'e7ade, which it considered sufficient to assert jurisdiction.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Anthony Fajardo, Development Services Department Director. Mr. Fajardo clarified that the property is subject to both a historic designation and a separate historic preservation easement with different boundaries, which contributes to confusion about the limits of the Board's oversight. In response to Mayor Trantalis' question, Mr. Fajardo confirmed that the artificial turf area is inclusive of the historic designated area.\par
\par
Commissioner Glassman explained his involvement and history of the site\rquote s historic designation. Commissioner Glassman commented on his viewpoint that the artificial turf installation would not alter the historic fa\'e7ade, the structure itself, or the public right-of-way and noted that the Board had previously approved more substantial additions to the site such as shade structures and awnings. He noted that the HPB's objection to a small area of artificial turf appears inconsistent. Based on those factors, Commissioner Glassman said this matter warrants reconsideration through a De Novo Hearing and expounded on his perspective. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
In response to City Attorney McCartney's question, Commissioner Glassman confirmed his recommendation for a De Novo Hearing based on the lack of \cf1 competent or substantial evidence.\par
\par
In response to Mayor Trantalis' question regarding whether staff had provided an opinion on whether the artificial turf installation interfered with the designated structure, Trisha Logan, Principal Urban Planner, said that most of the required criteria were not met, the artificial turf did not meet historic preservation criteria, is generally discouraged in historic districts, and said that natural grass would be more historically compatible. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
In response to Vice Mayor Herbst's questions regarding aspects of historic preservation relative to modern construction materials for needed renovations, Ms. Logan explained that modern materials may be allowed in historic settings if they maintain the appearance of the historic structure, Vice Mayor Herbst expressed concern about the subjective nature of determining acceptable substitutions and expounded on his perspective. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Commissioner Glassman introduced a resolution setting a De Novo Hearing for March 3, 2026, to hear this appeal based on insufficient evidence to support the decision of the HPB.\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\fs24 Commissioner Glassman requested staff provide an update on revisions that were incorporated into this Agenda item based on prior Commission discussion. Mayor Trantalis recognized Milos Majstorovic, Transportation and Mobility Department Director. Mr. Majstorovic discussed the Commission\rquote s earlier request for additional tree canopy coverage along the Las Olas corridor, particularly in the Shops segment and explained the substantial increase in tree canopy coverage across all Las Olas Boulevard corridor segments.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis provided an overview of this Agenda item and explained that Las Olas Boulevard is divided into three (3) distinct segments each with different design elements and improvements.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Sorensen's questions regarding widening the sidewalks in the Shops segment, Mr. Majstorovic explained that widening the sidewalks requires taking space from another part of the roadway, and the only way to significantly widen sidewalks would be to remove the median and its trees.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Sorensen's request for clarification regarding whether widening sidewalks along the Shops segment could occur while keeping the existing median and trees, Mr. Majstorovic explained that construction to expand the sidewalks would significantly compromise the root systems of the existing median trees that would likely not be preserved. City code and spatial constraints limit the types of trees that can be replanted in the median.\par
\cf0\par
\kerning2 Mayor Trantalis recognized Danella Williams, 540 SW 10th Avenue. Ms. Williams discussed her viewpoint regarding this Agenda item.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Ted Inserra, 901 SW 19th Street, River Oaks Civic Association President. Mr. Inserra discussed his opposition to this Agenda item. \par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Sally Alshouse, 1101 River Reach Drive. Ms. Alshouse discussed her opposition to this Agenda item.\par
\par
In response to Vice Mayor Herbst\rquote s question, staff confirmed the existing black olive trees in the median were planted in 1970. \par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Nick Ciani, 1529 NE 17th Terrace. Mr. Ciani discussed his viewpoint regarding this Agenda item.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Julianna Yonan, 1018 SW 20th Street. Ms. Yonan spoke in opposition to this Agenda item.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Evelyn Ciocco, 1515 E. Las Olas Boulevard. Ms. Ciocco spoke in opposition to this Agenda item.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Herbst clarified that the black olive trees along the Shops segment are not memorial trees. Memorial plantings in recognition of Veterans consist of palm trees in the residential, eastern segment of Las Olas Boulevard. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Douglas Herbst, 347 N. New River Drive East. Mr. Herbst discussed his viewpoint favoring maintaining parking along Las Olas Boulevard.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Payton DeLong, 511 SE 5th Avenue, Downtown Civic Association Member. Mr. DeLong spoke in support of this Agenda item and submitted a document for the record.\par
\par
\b\i A copy of the document is attached to these Meeting Minutes.\b0\i0\par
\par
Vice Mayor Herbst and Mr. DeLong discussed potential pedestrian-focused uses for the Shops section. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
\kerning0 Mayor Trantalis recognized Brucie Cummings, 830 SW 9\super th\nosupersub Street, on behalf of the Tarpon River Civic Association. Ms. Cummings spoke in opposition to removing the black olive trees.\par
\kerning2\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Charlie Ladd, 442 NE 7th Avenue, on behalf of the Las Olas Association and the Downtown Development Authority. Mr. Ladd spoke in support of this Agenda item.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recommended a targeted, segment-specific approach to improvements along Las Olas Boulevard, focusing on problem areas instead of applying uniform changes, cited examples, and expounded on his viewpoint. He also cautioned against overengineering an area that is performing well and expounded on his perspective. Further comment and discussion ensued regarding increased density in the City contributing to the success of Las Olas Boulevard.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Anne Hilmer, 621 Idlewyld Drive, on behalf of the Idlewyld Improvement Association (Association). Ms. Hilmer referenced actions taken by the Association's Board, noting that it had unanimously voted on multiple items, including updating a traffic study, concerns regarding emergency response times in Las Olas Isles, issues related to sidewalk caf\'e9s in the Shops segment, and emphasized the importance of maintaining the character of Las Olas Boulevard, including its trees and overall identity.\par
\par
\b\i A copy of the document is attached to these Meeting Minutes.\par
\pard\tx7164\b0\i0\par
In response to Vice Mayor Herbst\rquote s question, Ms. Hilmer outlined concerns about street parking on Las Olas Boulevard, citing Emergency Medical Service response times in the Isles and potential impacts on hurricane evacuation routes. Further comment and discussion ensued. Vice Mayor Herbst discussed street parking benefits, cited examples, and expounded on the Vision Zero goal to slow down traffic and reduce pedestrian fatalities. Ms. Hilmer remarked on Las Olas Boulevard outdoor cafes reducing sidewalk width.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Sorensen\rquote s questions, Chris Cooper, Deputy City Manager, said that several sidewalk caf\'e9s operate on public property along the Shops segment and clarified related information.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Chris Nelson, 520 SE 5th Avenue. Mr. Nelson spoke in opposition to this Agenda item.\par
\par
\pard Mayor Trantalis recognized Robert Lochrie, Esq., Lochrie and Chakas, P.A., on behalf of McTigue Family. Mr. Lochrie spoke in support of this Agenda item.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Hugh Johnson, 1119 N. Victoria Park Road. Mr. Johnson discussed his viewpoint regarding this Agenda item.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Esthel Brennan, 732 SW 13th Avenue. Ms. Brennan spoke in opposition to this Agenda item.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized John Roth, 333 Sunset Drive. Mr. Roth discussed his viewpoint regarding this Agenda item and submitted a document for the record.\par
\par
\b\i A copy of the document is attached to these Meeting Minutes.\b0\i0\par
\kerning0\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Mike Weymouth, The Las Olas Company President. Mr. Weymouth spoke in support of this Agenda item. In response to Vice Mayor Herbst's questions, Mr. Weymouth confirmed that the outdoor dining tables along Las Olas Boulevard are located on private property, not within the public right-of-way, and the City cannot reclaim those areas to widen sidewalks.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis discussed his perspective regarding sidewalk width and structural limitations in the Shops segment that vary by location. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Christine Demarco, 1315 Miami Road. Ms. Demarco spoke in opposition to this Agenda item.\par
\kerning2\b\i\par
\b0\i0 In response to Commissioner Sorensen's questions, Laura Tooley, Public Works Department Urban Forestry Supervisor, confirmed that sidewalk tree planting is feasible and has improved with modern infrastructure. Ms. Tooley said that larger, longer-living canopy trees are now possible. She said that oak trees are recommended for the redesigned sidewalk area of the Shops segment and discussed the anticipated oak tree height and canopy width. Commissioner Sorensen reviewed his understanding.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Glassman\rquote s questions, Ms. Tooley said that black olive trees are restricted because they have proven to be a poor long-term urban tree choice and commented on related details. City policy favors more resilient, canopy-producing species for future planting. Ms. Tooley confirmed that a six foot (6\rquote ) wide median is too constrained for canopy trees under current code requirements, and small ornamental trees or palms are viable, but would not contribute to shade or long-term canopy goals.\par
\par
\kerning0 In response to Commissioner Sorensen\rquote s questions, Ms. Tooley stated that the anticipated canopy or drip line from the proposed high-rise oak trees would be ten feet (10\rquote ). \par
\par
In response to Commissioner Sorensen\rquote s question about the anticipated high-rise oak canopy width, Walter Meyer, WSP Team Landscape Architect, explained that high-rise oak trees vertical growth reduce conflicts with buildings, sidewalks, and traffic corridors. Mr. Meyer said that high-rise oaks are expected to reach twenty feet (20\rquote ) in height with a twenty-foot (20\rquote ) canopy diameter, noting that these dimensions can vary based on environmental factors and remarked on examples.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Carlos Lang, 1243 SW 4th Avenue. Mr. Lang spoke in support of this Agenda item and retaining on-street parking.\par
\par
\kerning2 Mayor Trantalis recognized Mary Fertig, 511 Poinciana Drive. Ms. Fertig read from a prepared statement regarding her viewpoint on this Agenda item.\par
\par
\b\i A copy of the document is attached to these Meeting Minutes.\par
\kerning0\b0\i0\par
Mayor Trantalis addressed concerns raised by Ms. Fertig, including conflicts between traffic calming measures and streetscape improvements, emergency access, traffic congestion, street flooding, and infrastructure needs along Las Olas Boulevard. Ms. Fertig emphasized the importance of establishing firm project costs and building a stronger community consensus before moving forward.\par
\par
In response to Mayor Trantalis' question regarding the design of the Downtown segment, the Shops segment, and the Colee Hammock segment, Ms. Fertig confirmed her opposition to narrowing streets in any segment of Las Olas Boulevard, noted the need for flexibility, and confirmed her support of the Downtown Civic Association\rquote s position. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
In response to Vice Mayor Herbst's questions, Ms. Fertig confirmed that a potential compromise could include retaining parking lanes without bulb-outs to preserve flexibility for both daily use and emergency access vehicles and noted the need to implement these consistently along the segments.\par
\par
In response to Vice Mayor Herbst's comments and questions regarding evacuation routes and emergency response times for the Idlewyld neighborhood, Ms. Fertig noted that a primary concerns are fixed street design elements such as medians, bulb-outs, narrowed traffic lanes that cause pinch points and reduce the ability of drivers to clear a path for emergency vehicles. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
\kerning2 Mayor Trantalis recognized Michael Schneider, 139 Fiesta Way. Mr. Schneider spoke in opposition to this Agenda item and concurred with points discussed by Ms. Fertig.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Jenni Morejon, President and Chief Executive Officer, Fort Lauderdale Downtown Development Authority (DDA). Ms. Morejon spoke in support of this Agenda item.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Jennifer Peters, 420 NE 9th Avenue. Ms. Peters discussed her perspective regarding this Agenda item.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Steve Hudson, 1799 SE 9th Street. Mr. Hudson discussed his viewpoint in support of this Agenda item. In response to Commissioner Sorensen\rquote s question, Mr. Hudson confirmed his support of bulb-outs included in the proposed conceptual design.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Sorensen\rquote s question, Fire-Rescue Department Chief Stephen Gollan stated that the department strongly supports flexible, barrier-free street designs. He explained that fixed elements such as medians or rigid traffic calming features are seen as direct impediments to emergency response efficiency.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Joy Triglia, 2624 Marion Drive. Ms. Triglia spoke in opposition to this Agenda item.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Chris Stachowski, 500 SW 7th Street. Mr. Stachowski spoke in opposition to this Agenda item.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Francois Chidiac, 723 Bryan Place. Mr. Chidiac spoke in opposition to this Agenda item.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Robert Kimball, 1841 SW 22nd Street. Mr. Kimball spoke in opposition to this Agenda item.\par
\cf1\kerning0\par
There being no one else wishing to speak on this item, Commissioner Sorensen made a motion to close the public hearing and was seconded by Commissioner Glassman. Roll call showed AYES: Commissioner Glassman, Commissioner Beasley-Pittman, Commissioner Sorensen, Vice Mayor Herbst, and Mayor Trantalis.\par
\par
Commissioner Sorensen expressed support for the proposed design, highlighting its wider sidewalks as essential for a pedestrian-friendly environment that encourages shopping, dining and leisure, and remarked on how on-street parking benefits both businesses and residents.\par
\par
Commissioner Glassman said he would defer to Commissioner Sorensen as the District 4 Commissioner. Commissioner Glassman noted that he participated in a walking tour with the Downtown Civic Association Board of Directors focused on the area from Third Avenue to Tunnel Top Park, west of the Shops segment, which is included in this Agenda item. He remarked on his observations of the traffic patterns and sidewalk widths. \par
\par
In response to Commissioner Glassman's questions regarding whether it would be beneficial to remove on-street parking from SE Third Avenue to SE Sixth Avenue in the Downtown segment and whether there is flexibility to adjust the parking plan as design plans move forward, Mr. Majstorovic explained that the proposed plan provides two (2) travel lanes in each direction for that segment of the roadway, explaining the intent and that the outside lanes are used for parking. No design changes are required to allow or restrict parking and design changes can be addressed as an operational adjustment in the future. Mayor Trantalis confirmed his support of the Downtown segment noting the need for additional work to address design features.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Beasley-Pittman's question regarding sufficient community outreach regarding the redesign of Las Olas Boulevard, Mr. Majstorovic explained details of community outreach. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Beasley-Pittman's question regarding a Las Olas Boulevard parking study, Mr. Majstorovic said a parking study was not conducted. He explained the City's approach includes the installation of new technology designed to collect parking data, and expounded on related information. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Commissioner Beasley-Pittman made a motion to extend this meeting until 10:30 p.m. and was seconded by Commissioner Sorensen.\par
\par
\b APPROVED\par
\par
Yea: 5 \b0 - Commissioner Glassman, Commissioner Beasley-Pittman, Commissioner Sorensen, Vice Mayor Herbst and Mayor Trantalis\par
\par
\par
Commissioner Beasley-Pittman confirmed her continuing support for this Agenda item and expounded on her viewpoint. Commissioner Beasley-Pittman shared her perspective and ongoing concerns, and acknowledged prior Commission discussions supporting removal of the median, but remains concerned about neighbor opposition and emergency vehicle access along Las Olas Boulevard. Commissioner Beasley-Pittman commented on the extended duration of these discussions, rising costs, and her desire to prevent further delays and expenses.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Herbst commented on his recollection of discussions regarding this Agenda item and explained related details. Vice Mayor Herbst confirmed his support for proposed improvements, including widening the sidewalk, enhancing the pedestrian experience, increasing the shade canopy, and improving public safety by providing better access for police and fire vehicles. He noted his concerns about the rising costs of this project and its affordability, the need to obtain firm funding and possible funding opportunities, and expounded on his viewpoint. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis expressed support for a phased approach to the project. He recommends bifurcating this Agenda item and moving forward with the Downtown and Colee Hammock segments, where there is consensus, while pausing and refining the Shops segment due to ongoing concerns. He emphasized the importance of preserving the character of the Shops segment by maintaining the median trees and gradually introducing canopy trees along sidewalks. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Commissioner Sorensen introduced this Resolution which was read by title only.\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\fs24 Each Commission Member disclosed verbal communications, written communications, site visits, and expert opinions received.\par
\par
In response to Mayor Trantalis' question, City Attorney McCartney explained details of what the Commission Members must determine relative to this appeal.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis opened the public hearing.\par
\par
\cf0 Mayor Trantalis recognized Ellyn Bogdanoff, Esq., Becker & Poliakoff, P.A., One East Broward Boulevard on behalf of the applicant. Ms. Bogdanoff narrated a presentation entitled \i Appeal to the City of Fort Lauderdale Commission February 17, 2026 Agenda Item PH-126-0172 From the Board of Adjustment Tacher PLN-BOA-24040001\i0 .\par
\par
\b\i A copy of the presentation is attached to these Meeting Minutes.\b0\i0\par
\par
In response to Mayor Trantalis' questions, Ms. Bogdanoff clarified that the shed shown in the upper left-hand corner of the presentation, located on the water side, is rectangular and matches the structure and size originally installed in 2013. She explained that any apparent discrepancy results from the presentation's depiction, not an actual enlargement.\par
\par
\cf1 Vice Mayor Herbst questioned inconsistencies in the permit application for the pre-fabricated shed, noting that the document listed the structure as a 10'x10' unit, while evidence suggested it was actually a 10'x20' shed. Vice Mayor Herbst pointed out that the application appeared to be completed in consistent handwriting, raising doubts about whether the size discrepancy was an error or misrepresentation at the time of submission.\par
\par
Ms. Bogdanoff remarked on the discrepancy but emphasized that the shed had been permitted, inspected, and approved by the City at the time of installation under a prior owner. The current homeowners unknowingly inherited this issue and would have taken corrective action earlier had it been identified during the purchase process. Efforts to correct the issue were complicated by the need for variances, which were not initially obtained by the previous property owner. The current property owners are now facing significant financial hardship due to significant Code Enforcement fines. \par
\par
Ms. Bogdanoff requested approval of the requested four (4) variances to bring the property into compliance and asked that the accrued fines be waived. In response to Vice Mayor Herbst's question, Ms. Bogdanoff said that there has been no neighborhood opposition and that adjacent property owners have been supportive.\par
\cf0\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Hudson C. Gill, Esq., Johnson, Anselmo, Murdock, Burke, Piper & Hochman, P.A., on behalf of the City's Board of Adjustment (BOA). \cf1 In response to Commissioner Sorensen's question, City Attorney McCartney confirmed the City pays for the BOA's outside counsel.\par
\par
Mr. Gill clarified the Commission\rquote s role and the applicable legal standard for evaluating the variance requests. He explained that the burden of proof rests on the applicant, who must demonstrate by a preponderance of the evidence that a qualifying hardship exists under the Unified Land Development Regulations (ULDR).\par
\par
In response to Mayor Trantalis' question, Mr. Gill explained that the Commission should review the evidence to determine if the applicant meets all required criteria. These include whether special conditions affect the property and prevent reasonable use, whether these conditions are unique to the property, whether strict application of the ULDR would deprive the applicant of rights enjoyed by others in the district, whether the hardship was not self-created or due to ignorance of the code, and whether the requested variance is the minimum necessary and aligns with the intent of the ULDR. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis noted there were no members of the BOA present to contradict the facts presented by Ms. Bogdanoff. City Attorney McCartney explained the Commission cannot waive or modify fines. Only the Special Magistrate can waive and modify fines but the Commission can make a related recommendation.\par
\par
There being no one else wishing to speak on this item, Commissioner Sorensen made a motion to close the public hearing and was seconded by Commissioner Glassman. Roll call showed AYES: Commissioner Glassman, Commissioner Beasley-Pittman, Commissioner Sorensen, Vice Mayor Herbst, and Mayor Trantalis.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis said that the Commission, acting in a quasi-judicial capacity, must determine whether the applicant has satisfied all four (4) required hardship criteria based on the evidence presented, including submitted documents and photographs, and that their decision must be grounded strictly in that evidence.\par
\par
Commissioner Sorensen said a City permitting error was a key factor that created a unique hardship and moved to approve all four (4) variances, explaining related details, and said that the applicant met the ULDR criteria.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Glassman's question about including a recommendation to waive fines in the motion to approve the variances, Commissioner Sorensen suggested addressing fines separately.\par
\par
In response to Vice Mayor Herbst's questions about input from adjacent neighbors, Ms. Bogdanoff confirmed that one (1) nearby resident had expressed support for the applicant at a prior BOA hearing, explained related information, and said that no written objections or complaints had been filed. Ms. Bogdanoff also noted that a neighboring property had recently changed ownership, and the new owners had not raised concerns.\par
\par
City Attorney McCartney clarified that if the Commission intended to make any recommendation regarding fines, it would need to be explicitly included in a motion.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Herbst discussed waiving the accrued fines in conjunction with the variance approval and explained that, while fines can sometimes be reduced or waived, typically \ldblquote hard costs\rdblquote associated with enforcement activities such as inspections and staff time are not waived. Further comment and discussion ensued. \par
\par
Mayor Trantalis concurred with Vice Mayor Herbst's comment that hard costs incurred by the City should not be waived. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Commissioner Sorensen made a motion to approve the four (4) variances, reject the decision of the Board of Adjustment, and recommended sending this matter back to the Special Magistrate to waive the Code Enforcement fines minus the associated hard costs, and was seconded by Commissioner Glassman.\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\f0\fs24 City Manager Williams introduced this Agenda item and announced that Rachel Williams, Housing and Community Development Manager, would lead the discussion on the AHAC\rquote s recommendation to advance three (3) new affordable housing strategies and the previously discussed incentives. Ms. Williams narrated a presentation entitled \i CITY COMMISSION AND AFFORDABLE HOUSING ADVISORY COMMITTEE (AHAC) JOINT WORKSHOP.\par
\par
\b A copy of the presentation is part of the backup to this Agenda item.\par
\b0\par
\i0 Mayor Trantalis discussed concerns related to potential community opposition to reducing lot sizes in single-family neighborhoods as part of affordable housing incentives. In response to Mayor Trantalis' question regarding how to respond to those anticipated concerns, AHAC Chair Susan Spragg explained the genesis of this incentive and said that the current public land inventory process is ineffective, yielding no viable sites. AHAC is recommending expanded criteria and parameters, cited examples, and expounded on related examples as noted in the \i Affordable Housing Advisory Committee 2025 Affordable Housing Incentive Report \i0 (Report).\i\par
\i0\par
\b\i A copy of the Report is part of the backup to this Agenda item.\b0\i0\par
\par
Commissioner Beasley-Pittman clarified that this incentive aims to unlock development potential on existing nonconforming or irregular lots by allowing zoning flexibility to increase housing inventory. In response to Mayor Trantalis' question, AHAC Member Rich DeGirolamo stated that this incentive seeks an approach that respects neighborhood character and green space while implementing creative zoning and policy solutions to advance affordable housing inventory. Mayor Trantalis commented on tax incentives for affordable housing. Mr. DeGirolamo recommended that the City leverage its land assets and public-private partnership opportunities to develop a comprehensive, data-driven inventory identifying affordable housing opportunities. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
In response to Vice Mayor Herbst's questions regarding current minimum zoning lot size requirements, Chris Cooper, Deputy City Manager, said that single-family RS-8 and RS-4 zoning districts include minimum standards for both lot square footage and lot width and typical minimum lot sizes are around six thousand square feet (6,000 sq. ft.). He noted that many parcels are nonconforming, and in those instances property owners may seek relief through the Board of Adjustment, which has the authority to grant variances allowing development on lots that fall slightly below the required standards. Mr. Cooper noted the opportunity to revisit zoning regulations to better accommodate those parcels and meet goals based on Commission feedback. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Herbst commented on historical housing patterns, noting that smaller homes on smaller lots that accommodated large families and supported more affordable living. The trend toward larger homes and suburban sprawl has contributed to current housing affordability challenges. Vice Mayor Herbst expressed support for policies promoting smaller lots and denser, more modest housing. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Commissioner Sorensen expressed support for incentivizing workforce and affordable housing. In response to Commissioner Sorensen's question regarding whether zoning variances allowing reduced lot sizes could be conditioned upon the inclusion of affordable or workforce housing units, Mr. Cooper said such an approach would be a Commission policy decision and acknowledged that tying affordability requirements to variance approvals could be considered a potential justification for allowing deviations from existing land development regulations. Commissioner Sorensen commented on his support for expanding affordable housing strategies to include commercial and industrial properties. Mr. Cooper commented on viable opportunities to expand affordable housing through commercial, industrial, and mixed-use development by leveraging City-owned land and CRA partnerships. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
City Manager Williams emphasized the need to establish clear criteria for incentivizing affordable housing developments and Commission policies that clearly define key components.\par
\par
Commissioner Sorensen expressed support for targeting affordable housing incentives at fifty percent (50%) of Area Median Income (AMI), noting that this threshold is more aligned with local housing needs in contrast to the State\rquote s Live Local Act, which allows eligibility up to one hundred twenty percent (120%) of AMI. He suggested that the lower AMI target represents a more meaningful and impactful definition for community affordability.\par
\par
Mr. Cooper said that upcoming updates on accessory dwelling units (ADUs) would include considerations related to minimum lot size requirements, which are directly connected to the broader discussion on zoning flexibility and smaller lots. In response to Commissioner Glassman's question regarding latest State legislative developments regarding ADUs, Mr. Cooper said an update would be forthcoming.\par
\par
Commissioner Beasley-Pittman recommended that AMI percentages should be clearly translated into dollar values to improve public understanding of the realities of income levels tied to affordable housing policies.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis discussed the need to be mindful that the small infill lot strategy to address affordable housing is nearing its limits, and said future efforts with bigger lots will likely need to shift toward larger, more complex developments such as multifamily or mixed-use projects. Further comment and discussion ensued. Mr. Cooper noted that future infill lot opportunities may be limited, but AHAC wants a more formal role in evaluating and advising on available infill parcels to maximize affordable housing potential.\par
\par
In response to Mayor Trantalis' question regarding public awareness of affordable housing opportunities, Kevin Pulido, Strategic Communications Office Director, said staff can significantly improve public awareness by proactively using its communication channels and community networks to better inform residents about available units and the application process. Commissioner Beasley-Pittman discussed her viewpoint regarding the affordable housing audience and noted the need for stronger, more visible outreach such as electronic signage and targeted communications to ensure local residents are aware of and can access affordable housing opportunities. Commissioner Sorensen recommended establishing a periodic, structured communication system to notify the public of infill parcel availability that will improve transparency, coordination and public awareness of affordable housing opportunities, and cited examples. City Manager Williams confirmed.\par
\par
Commissioner Beasley-Pittman emphasized the importance of expanding affordable housing public awareness and education efforts particularly through first-time home buyer workshops. Staff should expand its role in hosting first-time home buyer education programs to help residents and employees access homeownership. Rachel Williams confirmed.\par
\par
Chair Spragg discussed developing an Affordable Housing Master Plan (AHMP), remarked on Broward County's housing needs assessment, and recommended a City-specific housing assessment and master plan to provide more targeted data and an improved affordable housing strategy. Chair Spragg said that AHAC was selected by the Florida Housing Coalition for a support initiative that will result in an in-depth analysis of the City\rquote s land development regulations, prior AHAC reports, and existing housing policies. AHAC\rquote s selection provides an opportunity to refine policies, identify best practices, and develop a comprehensive, data-driven housing strategy, including partnerships to support workforce housing. Commissioner Sorensen confirmed his support of that initiative.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Sorensen's question regarding the cost to develop an AHMP, Ms. Williams remarked on the $60,000 cost for a housing needs assessment in 2019. Mayor Trantalis discussed his perspective and questioned the need for further studies, emphasizing that the affordability crisis is already clear and that affordable housing production is largely driven by developer feasibility and available incentives. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
In response to Mayor Trantalis' question, Ms. Williams explained the current affordable housing gap need is fifty percent (50%) of AMI and financial feasibility is hardest, requiring stronger or more creative incentives to attract development. Mayor Trantalis agreed, expounded on his viewpoint, and cited examples.\par
\par
Commissioner Beasley-Pittman said that the City should proactively engage successful, repeat developers to contribute to fifty percent (50%) of AMI affordable housing needs and expounded on her viewpoint. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Ms. Williams noted the need for affordable housing incentives to be designed to prioritize households most at risk of homelessness, with clear policy direction from the Commission to guide those efforts.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis referenced a recent opinion piece by a local architect in the \i Sun Sentinel \i0 discussing affordable and lower-income housing and the role cities can play in incentivizing private development to achieve those goals. He said that this article was relevant to the City\rquote s ongoing discussion about policy direction. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
In response to Mayor Trantalis' questions regarding AMI levels that should be prioritized, Ms. Williams clarified that while the market is already producing projects in the eighty percent (80%) AMI and above range, the Commission is being asked for a clear policy choice between supporting existing market trends of eighty percent plus (80%+) AMI or prioritizing AMI rates below eighty percent (80%).\par
\par
Commissioner Sorensen noted his support of deeper affordability levels below eighty percent (80%) of AMI.\par
\par
City Manager Williams suggested fifteen percent (15%) or twenty percent (20%) of units in mixed-income development proposals should be designated as affordable for households at eighty percent (80%) or below AMI as benchmarks for future incentive programs. Mayor Trantalis recommended a multi-tiered, mixed-income approach that includes rental units at forty percent (40%) to sixty percent (60%) of AMI, sixty percent (60%) to eight percent (80%) of AMI, and an eighty percent (80%) to one hundred twenty percent (120%) of AMI to create financially viable projects while addressing a broader range of housing needs, which would retain residents across numerous income levels. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Commissioner Beasley-Pittman said that an affordable housing policy should reflect changing demographics, particularly seniors and working residents, and take a more inclusive approach to prevent housing instability and homelessness. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Commissioner Sorensen suggested a policy targeting households at forty percent (40%) to sixty percent (60%) of AMI with a benchmark of fifty percent (50%) of AMI rental units within a development. Mayor Trantalis noted that may not be realistic. In response to Mayor Trantalis' question, Mr. Cooper concurred and noted that target would likely be too high to be financially viable for developers. \par
\par
City Manager Williams recommended establishing a target designating approximately twenty percent (20%) of rental units as affordable with flexibility based on project feasibility and evaluation of each project\rquote s financial structure. Commissioner Beasley-Pittman noted the need to move away from the current ten percent (10%) benchmark. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Mr. Cooper requested Commission feedback on staff continuing to advance the ADU policy initiative. AHAC, in coordination with Housing and Community Development, Community Services, and Development Services Department, developed an ADU action plan focused on education, streamlined approvals, code updates, and tracking. \par
\par
Vice Mayor Herbst said that the State Legislature is actively considering regulations related to ADUs, including provisions that would restrict their use as short-term rentals. Vice Mayor Herbst noted the importance of monitoring these legislative developments and cautioned against finalizing local ADU policies until direction has been received from the State to ensure alignment. Mr. Cooper agreed and explained related information. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
In response to Mayor Trantalis' questions, Mr. Cooper explained that ADUs are currently allowed and could serve as an affordable housing tool, noting emerging lower-cost construction methods that improve their feasibility. Vice Mayor Herbst said the City should consider more flexible ADU size and design standards to allow smaller, more efficient units that better meet diverse housing needs, particularly for seniors and their families.\par
\par
Mr. Cooper requested Commission direction regarding staff pursuing policy allowing certain impact fees to be waived for affordable housing developments. In response to Vice Mayor Herbst's question, Mr. Cooper confirmed that recent State legislation allows for a full waiver of certain impact fees for affordable housing developments. Implementing waivers would require amendments to the Code and the waiver program would be structured as part of a broader, layered incentive strategy applied selectively on a case-by-case basis to support a development project's affordable housing components. The waiver program would apply only to the affordable portion of a development, while market-rate units would still be subject to standard impact fees. Mr. Cooper clarified the need for additional policy design, financial considerations, and legal review before implementation.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Herbst expressed concern that waiving water and wastewater impact fees could conflict with associated infrastructure bond funding covenants as these fees are often pledged to service debt. Mr. Cooper acknowledged that this issue has not yet been fully analyzed and is a critical consideration that will need to be evaluated as part of developing any fee waiver policy.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Glassman's questions about the potential revenue impact of waiving impact fees for affordable housing projects, Yvette Matthews, Assistant City Manager, provided an example of an eighty-eight (88) unit affordable housing development serving households below sixty percent (60%) AMI that could receive approximately $148,000 in waived fees. Ms. Matthews clarified that impact fee revenues fluctuate annually based on development activity. Park impact fees typically generate between $2,000,000 and $4,000,000 per year, while water and wastewater impact fees range from $1,800,000 to $5,000,000 annually. The specific portion of these revenues attributable to affordable housing projects is currently not known. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis discussed his perspective and said that while impact fee waivers can be an incentive for affordable housing, the lost revenue would need to be offset and requires careful policy design and safeguards, such as caps to manage the financial impact.\par
\par
Commissioner Glassman noted that this is Chair Spragg's last meeting and expressed appreciation for her service and contributions to the AHAC.\cf1\f1\par
}

Ms. Jacob discussed ongoing noise concerns from Fort Lauderdale Executive Airport (FXE) that negatively affect her neighborhood. She referenced her aviation expertise as a Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) licensed commercial pilot and described sustained efforts to collaborate with staff on noise abatement. Ms. Jacob requested an updated aircraft noise study and proactive mitigation measures, noting that current data is outdated and that forthcoming airport changes could exacerbate noise impacts.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Rufus James, Fort Lauderdale Executive Airport Director. Mr. James responded to Ms. Jacob\rquote s concerns, stating that the last formal FAA Part 150 Noise Study at FXE (Noise Study) was conducted in 2002 and remarked on related information.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Herbst stated that relying on a nearly twenty-five-year-old noise study is inadequate and emphasized the need for the City to conduct an updated analysis. City Manager Williams concurred, acknowledging that the 2002 Noise Study is outdated.\par
\par
In response to Vice Mayor Herbst\rquote s questions, Ms. Jacob referenced her November 2024 comments to the Commission regarding proactive noise mitigation efforts at FXE, which were well-received. She explained that, under the Noise Study framework, modifications to airport layout and perimeter design could reduce noise impacts, and recommended considering alternatives such as berms and blast pads. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
In response to Vice Mayor Herbst\rquote s inquiry regarding noise mitigation efforts the City could undertake without FAA involvement, Mr. James stated that measures affecting aircraft navigation and operations would require federal oversight and must be evaluated as part of a Noise Study.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Herbst concluded that conducting an updated noise study should be the initial step, with mitigation measures to be implemented based on its findings. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Herbst requested that City Manager Williams provide a clear timeline for completing an updated Noise Study so that accurate expectations can be communicated to residents. He said that establishing a defined timeline would help manage expectations, giving the community a realistic understanding of the process while also creating internal accountability for staff to provide progress updates. City Manager Williams confirmed. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\fs24 Each Commission Member disclosed verbal communications, written communications, site visits, and expert opinions received.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis opened the public hearing.\par
\par
Commissioner Glassman expressed support for the site plan and requested clarification on the project's overall status, specifically regarding outstanding lease agreements, financing, and parking. Commissioner Glassman noted concerns about current economic uncertainty and market conditions, and inquired about their potential impact on the project's financial viability.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized William Brown, 112 N. Birch Road, Central Beach Alliance (CBA) President. Mr. Brown spoke in support of this Agenda item.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Stephanie Toothaker, Esq., 901 Ponce de Leon Drive, on behalf of Hall of Fame Partners, LLC (Applicant). Ms. Toothaker said she was available to answer questions about the site plan and parking, but deferred questions about the lease and financial matters to Mario Caprini. \par
\par
Mayor Trantalis recognized Mario Caprini, ISHOF Manager, Capital Group P3 Developments of Florida. In response to Commissioner Glassman\rquote s questions, Mr. Caprini stated that recent global events have increased financial market volatility and uncertainty, with rising interest rates creating urgency to secure financing. He discussed ongoing communications with City Manager Williams and staff, who indicated alignment on proceeding. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
City Manager Williams clarified that Mr. Caprini has been advised that they may proceed with securing a rate lock, contingent upon Commission approval of the site plan under consideration. \par
\par
In response to Mayor Trantalis\rquote question, Mr. Caprini confirmed that if the Commission approves the site plan, the developer intends to move forward immediately by locking in interest rates tomorrow. \par
\par
In response to Commissioner Glassman\rquote s question regarding additional details to be addressed, Mr. Caprini remarked on additional outstanding items expected to be resolved next week.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Glassman\rquote s question about media reports on parking, Ms. Toothaker explained that the project underwent significant design changes based on community feedback, particularly from the swimming community and neighboring condominiums. Removing two floors from the western building reduced the building's height and visual impact, but also reduced the number of parking spaces.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Glassman\rquote s questions regarding project parking, Ms. Toothaker stated that the number of parking spaces is determined by the site\rquote s varied uses. The site requires a total of four hundred and five (405) parking spaces, as specified by the City\rquote s Unified Land Development Regulations (ULDR). City-related functions, including the Aquatic Complex, pools, Ocean Rescue, and staff offices, require one hundred seventy-six (176) spaces. The west building requires two hundred twenty-nine (229) spaces, allocated as follows: sixty-one (61) for the museum, forty-three (43) for the aquarium, sixty-three (63) for events, and sixty-two (62) for the restaurant. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Commissioner Glassman suggested reinstating a shuttle service from the Las Olas Garage to the project to help manage peak parking demand and improve access. He noted that such a service would be particularly valuable during high-demand periods. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
City Manager Williams explained that funding previously allocated for the Las Olas Garage shuttle service was redirected to support the Circuit MicroTransit Program. Future consideration of reinstating the shuttle service would depend on operational needs, usage levels, and financial feasibility. Staff could also explore partnerships to offset potential costs. Commissioner Glassman agreed, noting that while the need is not immediate, it is important to keep this option in mind as the project progresses and shuttle demands evolve.\par
\par
Commissioner Glassman raised concerns, based on constituent complaints, regarding the condition and maintenance of the Aquatic Complex pools and cited specific examples. He emphasized the need to verify these concerns and ensure proper facility upkeep, stressing that, given the City\rquote s investment, the pools must be maintained to a high standard.\par
\par
City Manager Williams acknowledged receiving a related email and confirmed that staff would follow up to investigate and address those concerns.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis expressed concern about limited parking at the aquarium due to anticipated visitor volume and confirmed support for the proposed shuttle service. Ms. Toothaker agreed and stated that parking and access strategies would be adjusted based on actual usage once the facility is operational. The aquarium will implement a timed entry system to stagger arrivals and manage peak demand. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Herbst stated for the record that reducing building height at the expense of parking may be a mistake, citing past examples, despite community input that led to the reduction in building height.\par
\par
Commissioner Glassman explained that the design changes were made in response to extensive community feedback to balance stakeholder input and reduce the project\rquote s visual and operational impact. He cited examples regarding scale, aesthetics, and compatibility with surrounding uses, and further elaborated on his viewpoint. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Mayor Trantalis stated that parking challenges could be addressed through off-site parking, improved traffic circulation, and enhanced transportation options such as shuttles and the Circuit MicroTransit Service connecting the Las Olas garage with the Aquatic Center, which could be considered a viable operational expense. He also encouraged the City to consider reinstating its broader beach shuttle service.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Herbst warned that parking constraints could negatively affect project revenue and place the City at financial risk as the project guarantor. He urged prioritizing project viability over design preferences and further elaborated on his viewpoint. Further comment and discussion ensued.\par
\par
Commissioner Glassman suggested partnering with nearby hotels to utilize their underused parking facilities, which could provide a practical solution to address parking shortages and offer additional revenue for the hotels.\par
\par
There being no one else wishing to speak on this item, Commissioner Glassman made a motion to close the public hearing and was seconded by Commissioner Sorensen. Roll call showed AYES: Commissioner Sorensen, Vice Mayor Herbst, Commissioner Glassman, and Mayor Trantalis. NOT PRESENT: Commissioner Pamela Beasley-Pittman.\par
\par
Commissioner Glassman introduced this Resolution for approval which was read by title only.\par
}
